expert.content:
How to study Spring Core

• Spring looks like magic until you know its three mechanisms: the container (creates and wires objects), post-processors (modify definitions and instances) and proxies (add behaviour like transactions, security, async around your beans). Almost every annotation you use (@Autowired, @Transactional, @Async, @Cacheable, @Value) is implemented by one of them.
• Study by experiment: run small AnnotationConfigApplicationContext programs, print bean names, add logging BeanPostProcessors, turn on logging.level.org.springframework=DEBUG, and inspect proxies with AopUtils. Seeing the container do its work removes the mystery.

interviewQA: Which Spring Core topics matter most for interviews?

IoC and dependency injection (constructor injection), BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext, bean scopes and lifecycle, @Configuration/@Bean and stereotypes, @Autowired/@Qualifier/@Primary, BeanPostProcessor and BeanFactoryPostProcessor, AOP with JDK vs CGLIB proxies, @Transactional (propagation, isolation, self-invocation), profiles, events, SpEL and circular dependencies.
What mechanisms explain most of Spring's "magic"?

The IoC container that creates and wires beans, post-processors that customise bean definitions and instances, and proxies that wrap beans to add cross-cutting behaviour such as transactions and security.

topics.name: Spring Introduction & IoC

beginner.content:
What is a Framework?

A framework provides the common, repetitive plumbing that every application needs, so you only write the part that is specific to your business. Spring is such a framework for Java, created by Rod Johnson and released in 2003.

Advantages of the Spring Framework

AdvantageMeaning
Predefined templatesReady-made templates for JDBC, JPA, Hibernate and more. With JdbcTemplate you do not write code for opening the connection, creating the statement, handling SQLException or closing anything - you write the query and nothing else.
Loose couplingObjects receive their collaborators through dependency injection instead of creating them, so a class is never welded to one concrete implementation.
Easy to testA plain Spring application needs no server. A JDK and the Spring jars are enough to run and unit-test it.
LightweightSpring beans are POJOs. Your class is not forced to extend a framework base class or implement a framework interface.
Fast developmentConfiguration, wiring and boilerplate are handled by the container, so far less code is written per feature.

Tight Coupling vs Loose Coupling

This is the single idea the whole framework is built on, so it is worth being precise about it.

Tightly coupled: class A creates a B with new. A now depends on that exact class. Swapping B for a different implementation means editing and recompiling A.

Loosely coupled: A holds a reference of the interface type. Any class implementing that interface can be supplied. Swapping the implementation changes only what is handed in, never A itself.

Spring IoC (Spring Core)

IoC stands for Inversion of Control, and Spring Core is the base module every other Spring module is built on. The IoC container is responsible for three things: it instantiates your objects, configures them, and assembles them into a working object graph.

Why do we need it?

Without a container, every time you need a different collaborator you edit Java code:

Today   ->  B b = new B();     // hard-coded in class A
Tomorrow->  C c = new C();     // edit A, recompile, redeploy

Every change of collaborator is a change to Java source. Inversion of Control turns this around: you hand control of object creation to Spring. Your class declares what it needs; the container decides which object to supply and creates it on your behalf. You stop worrying about object creation entirely.

Why a container?

To pass any input into your POJO classes from outside the code - values, other beans, environment-specific settings - something has to read that configuration and apply it. That is the container's job.

What the IoC container actually does

StepWhat happens
1. Read configurationParses the XML configuration file (or the annotated classes) that declares your beans.
2. Instantiate beansCreates the object of every declared bean class.
3. Manage the lifecycleControls creation, initialisation, and destruction of each bean.
4. Inject valuesPasses the configured parameters and collaborating beans into each bean.

The Two IoC Containers

Spring ships two container types. Both hold a collection of beans; they differ in when the beans get created and in what else they can do.

1. BeanFactory - the core container

Used for standalone applications - the kind you install on each machine, like a calculator, a media player, or an antivirus. XmlBeanFactory is its implementation class, and its constructor takes a Resource, so a resource object must be created first.

2. ApplicationContext - the J2EE container

Used for web applications - the kind accessed through a browser. ClassPathXmlApplicationContext is its implementation class, and its constructor takes the configuration file name directly as a String.

Internal Working: BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext

BeanFactory - lazy
• The bean object is created at the moment the user calls getBean().
• It is called lazy because creation waits for the request.
• Nothing is created at loading time.

ApplicationContext - eager
• Bean objects are created at class-loading time, before any request arrives.
• It is called eager for exactly that reason.
• Declare ten beans and all ten are instantiated up front - provided their scope is singleton.
• If the scope is prototype, nothing is created at loading time.

PointDetail
Prototype scopeIn BOTH containers, a prototype-scoped bean is created fresh per request - never at startup.
Private constructorsSpring creates the instance whether the constructor is public or private; it uses reflection either way.
Default scopesingleton - one shared instance per container.

Fresher Notes

  • Spring is a Java framework that manages objects (beans) and their dependencies so your classes stay simple and loosely coupled.
  • IoC (Inversion of Control) means the container creates and wires objects instead of your code calling new.
  • The container is the ApplicationContext; it reads configuration (annotations, Java config or XML) and builds the beans.

Worked Example 1

Lifecycle callbacks.

Worked Example 2

Prototype scope.

Practice Exercise 1

Create a context and get a bean.

Practice Exercise 2

Component scanning.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

On startup the container reads bean definitions (from @Configuration/@Bean, scanned @Component classes or XML) into BeanDefinition objects, runs BeanFactoryPostProcessors, then instantiates singletons in dependency order. For each bean it resolves constructor arguments, injects properties, calls aware callbacks, runs BeanPostProcessors (this is where proxies for AOP and @Transactional are created), calls init methods and registers destroy callbacks.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Configuration styles: annotations and component scanning, Java config (explicit and testable), XML (legacy), and imports/profiles to combine them. Scopes: singleton, prototype, request, session, application, websocket. Conditional beans with @Profile, @Conditional, @ConditionalOnProperty (Boot).

expert.content:
IoC and Dependency Injection Are Not the Same Thing

The two words are used interchangeably in conversation, and interviewers like to separate them.

Inversion of Control is the broad principle: the framework, not your code, controls the flow and the creation of objects. Dependency Injection is one specific technique for achieving it - supplying a collaborator from outside rather than constructing it inside. Service Locator is a different technique for the same principle.

So: DI is a way to implement IoC, and it is the way Spring chose.

Where the container actually lives in a modern application

The XML and XmlBeanFactory above are the historical, teaching form of the container and remain the clearest way to see what it does. In current code the same container is created for you:

EraHow the container is created
Spring 2.x-3.x (XML)You write new ClassPathXmlApplicationContext("spring.xml") and declare every bean in XML.
Spring 3.x+ (Java config)new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(AppConfig.class) with @Configuration and @Bean methods - no XML.
Spring BootSpringApplication.run(App.class, args) creates and returns the same ApplicationContext; component scanning and auto-configuration fill it.

Note on XmlBeanFactory: it has been deprecated since Spring 3.1 and removed in Spring 5, in favour of DefaultListableBeanFactory with an XmlBeanDefinitionReader. You will still meet XmlBeanFactory in course material and legacy code, which is why it is shown here - but do not reach for it in new work.

Eager vs Lazy - Why the Default Is Eager

It looks wasteful to build every singleton at startup, and it is deliberate. If a bean is misconfigured - a missing dependency, a bad property, an unresolvable type - eager creation means the application fails at startup, in front of the developer or the deployment pipeline. Lazy creation means it fails on the first user request, in production.

Fail-fast at startup is the trade Spring makes: slightly slower boot in exchange for never shipping a container that cannot build its own beans.

SettingEffect
defaultEvery singleton is instantiated during context refresh.
lazy-init="true" on one beanThat single bean waits until it is first requested.
spring.main.lazy-initialization=true (Boot)Every bean becomes lazy. Cuts startup time; moves configuration errors to runtime.
@LazyThe annotation form, on a @Bean method, a @Component, or an injection point.

Bean Scopes

Scope decides how many instances of a bean the container hands out.

ScopeMeaning
singletonDefault. One instance per container, shared by everyone who asks for it. Created eagerly by ApplicationContext.
prototypeA brand-new instance for every getBean() call and every injection point. Never created at startup.
requestWeb only. One instance per HTTP request.
sessionWeb only. One instance per HTTP session.
applicationWeb only. One instance per ServletContext.

A trap worth knowing: "singleton" here means one per Spring container, not the Gang-of-Four Singleton pattern. Two containers in the same JVM each hold their own instance, and the class has no private constructor or getInstance().

A second trap: injecting a prototype bean into a singleton gives you one prototype instance, captured when the singleton was built. The singleton is only wired once. To get a fresh instance per call you need ObjectProvider, a lookup method, or @Scope(proxyMode = TARGET_CLASS).
codeExamples:
<!-- spring.xml -->
<bean id="emp" class="com.test.Employee" scope="prototype">
    <property name="firstName" value="ram"/>
</bean>
<!-- OUTPUT: -->
<!-- Nothing is created at startup. Every getBean("emp") builds a new Employee. -->

expert.content:
The Bean Lifecycle

"The container manages the lifecycle of your bean" means a defined sequence of callbacks runs around every bean. Knowing the order explains why initialisation logic belongs in @PostConstruct and not in the constructor.

Bean definition read from XML / @Configuration / component scan
        |
        v
Constructor called  (constructor injection happens here)
        |
        v
Setter / field injection of the remaining dependencies
        |
        v
Aware callbacks   (BeanNameAware, ApplicationContextAware, ...)
        |
        v
BeanPostProcessor.postProcessBeforeInitialization()
        |
        v
@PostConstruct  ->  InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()  ->  init-method
        |
        v
BeanPostProcessor.postProcessAfterInitialization()   <-- AOP proxies created here
        |
        v
        BEAN IS READY AND IN USE
        |
        v
@PreDestroy  ->  DisposableBean.destroy()  ->  destroy-method   (singletons only)

The constructor runs before setter-injected dependencies exist, which is precisely why code that touches an injected field must live in @PostConstruct. It is also why AOP proxies - transactions, security, caching - are applied at the post-initialisation step and never inside the bean's own constructor.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Who created Spring and when?Rod Johnson, 2003, out of the code in his book Expert One-on-One J2EE Design and Development.
What does IoC stand for and what does the container do?Inversion of Control. The container instantiates, configures and assembles your objects, and manages their lifecycle, instead of your code doing it with new.
Difference between IoC and DI?IoC is the principle - the framework controls object creation and flow. DI is the technique Spring uses to implement it: dependencies are supplied from outside rather than constructed inside.
Why is Spring called lightweight?Beans are POJOs - no framework base class to extend, no framework interface to implement, so the application code stays free of Spring types.
BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext?BeanFactory is the bare core container and creates singletons lazily on getBean(). ApplicationContext extends it, creates singletons eagerly at startup, and adds i18n, event publishing, resource loading and AOP support.
Which one would you use today?ApplicationContext, effectively always. BeanFactory is an internal detail; Spring Boot gives you an ApplicationContext from SpringApplication.run().
Why are singletons created eagerly by default?Fail-fast. A misconfigured bean breaks startup, where a developer sees it, instead of breaking the first production request.
Is a prototype bean created at startup?No. In both containers a prototype instance is created per request, never during context refresh.
Can Spring instantiate a class with a private constructor?Yes - it uses reflection, so constructor visibility does not stop it.
Is Spring's singleton scope the same as the Singleton design pattern?No. Spring's is one instance per container; the GoF pattern is one instance per class loader enforced by the class itself.
What happens if you inject a prototype bean into a singleton?The singleton is wired once, so it keeps one prototype instance forever. Use ObjectProvider, a lookup method, or a scoped proxy to get a fresh one per call.
Is XmlBeanFactory still used?No - deprecated in Spring 3.1 and removed in Spring 5. The replacement is DefaultListableBeanFactory loaded by an XmlBeanDefinitionReader.

Mid-Level Notes

  • A bean is any object managed by the container; by default it is a singleton per container.
  • Configure with @Component and component scanning, @Configuration classes with @Bean methods, or XML.
  • Benefits: easier testing (swap dependencies), centralized configuration, lifecycle management and AOP support.

Senior Notes

  • Understand the bean lifecycle: instantiate, populate dependencies, aware callbacks, post processors, init method, ready, destroy.
  • Scopes: singleton (default), prototype, request, session, application; choose by statefulness.
  • Spring Boot builds on Spring Core with auto-configuration; knowing the container explains most Boot behaviour.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: new-ing a bean yourself (not managed: no injection, no proxy), singleton beans holding mutable per-request state (thread-safety bugs), injecting a prototype into a singleton and expecting new instances, and expensive work in constructors that slows startup. Keep singletons stateless.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Startup time grows with bean count and classpath scanning. Narrow component scans, use lazy initialization for rarely used beans, and measure startup. Singleton access after startup is just a map lookup, so runtime cost is negligible.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a layered application. Controllers depend on services, services on repositories and gateways, all as interfaces, wired by the container. Replacing a gateway in tests or per environment needs no changes in the services.

topics.name: First Simple Spring Application

beginner.content:
What You Need

Three pieces build the first Spring application, and nothing else:

PiecePurpose
Spring bean class (.java)A plain POJO with private fields and getters/setters. This is the object the container will create for you.
Spring configuration file (.xml)Declares the bean and the values to inject into it.
Main application class (.java)Creates the container, asks it for the bean, and uses it.

Internal Working of Spring

STARTUP
  1.1  BeanFactory object is created
  1.2  The Spring configuration file is injected into the BeanFactory
  1.3  Spring bean (POJO) object is created and stored inside the IoC container

REQUEST
  2.1  getBean() is invoked from your main method
  2.2  The container looks up and returns the Student object
  2.3  The bean object is handed to your program

Two notes:
1. If you use ApplicationContext instead, an ApplicationContext object is created rather than a BeanFactory - the rest of the flow is identical.
2. The configuration file may be named spring.xml, applicationContext.xml, or anything else; you pass whatever name you chose.

Maven - the Build Automation Tool

Maven is a project management tool based on the POM (Project Object Model). It handles the build, the dependencies and the documentation of a project.

Why Maven?

Adding jars by hand is painful and error-prone. With Spring or Hibernate you must match exact, compatible versions across a dozen jars, and one mismatch produces a runtime failure that is hard to trace. Instead you declare a dependency in pom.xml; Maven downloads the jar from the central repository, stores it in your local repository, and adds it to the project.

What is pom.xml?

It holds the project information and the configuration Maven needs to build it - dependencies, build directory, source directory, test source directory, plugins and goals.

ElementMeaning
projectThe root element of the pom.xml file.
modelVersionSub-element of project. Set to 4.0.0.
groupIdThe id of the project group - unique across the organisation.
artifactIdThe project name.
versionThe project version, e.g. 0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.

Steps to Create the Spring Maven Project

1. Create a new project
2. Create the Spring bean class
3. Add the Maven dependencies to pom.xml
4. Create the test class with the main method
5. Create the spring.xml file
6. Run the Spring application
7. Check the output

Step 1 - Create a New Project

File -> New -> Other -> type Maven Project in the wizard -> Next. Tick Create a simple project, click Next, then enter spring as the Group Id and SpringDemoExample as the Artifact Id, and click Finish.

FieldMeaning
Group IdThe project id, unique throughout the application.
Artifact IdThe project name.

Step 2 - Create the Spring Bean Class

A POJO with private fields and public getters and setters. Nothing in it refers to Spring.

Step 3 - Add the Maven Dependencies

spring-core gives you the IoC container itself; spring-context adds ApplicationContext on top of it. The version is declared once as a property so both stay in step.
codeExamples:
<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-core</artifactId>
        <version>${spring.version}</version>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-context</artifactId>
        <version>${spring.version}</version>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

<properties>
    <spring.version>4.2.3.RELEASE</spring.version>
</properties>

beginner.content:
Step 4 - Create the Test Class with the main Method

This is where the container is created and the bean is fetched. getBean("s") uses the same id that the XML declares.

Step 5 - Create the spring.xml File

Always create the XML file in src/main/resources, nowhere else - that is the folder Maven puts on the classpath, and ClassPathResource looks there.

5.1 Right-click src/main/resources then New -> Other
5.2 Type xml in the wizard search box
5.3 Scroll down and select XML File
5.4 Click Next
5.5 Type spring in place of NewFile, click Next
5.6 Click Next
5.7 Click Finish

Each <property> element names a field and the value to set on it. Spring calls the matching setter for you.
codeExamples:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<beans xmlns="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans"
       xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
       xsi:schemaLocation="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans
                           http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans/spring-beans.xsd">

    <bean id="s" class="com.test.Student">
        <property name="firstName" value="ram"></property>
        <property name="age" value="25"></property>
        <property name="city" value="pune"></property>
    </bean>

</beans>

beginner.content:
Steps 6 and 7 - Run It and Check the Output

Open the Test class, then Right click -> Run As -> Java Application.

Fresher Notes

  • A first Spring application needs a Maven or Gradle project with spring-context, a bean class, a configuration and a main class that starts the context.
  • Define beans with @Component or @Bean and fetch them from the ApplicationContext.
  • Run it with your IDE or mvn exec:java.

Worked Example 1

Context test.

Worked Example 2

Constructor injected service.

Practice Exercise 1

Pom and main class.
codeExamples:
<dependency><groupId>org.springframework</groupId><artifactId>spring-context</artifactId><version>6.1.5</version></dependency>

@Configuration @ComponentScan
public class App {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var ctx = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(App.class);
        ctx.getBean(OrderService.class).place("A1", 2);
    }
}

// OUTPUT:
// order placed: A1 x2

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Properties.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Running new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(App.class) triggers a sequence: register the configuration class, process annotations (@ComponentScan, @Import, @Bean), create bean definitions, instantiate singletons, and publish ContextRefreshedEvent. If a dependency is missing or ambiguous, startup fails with a message that names the bean and the missing type.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Project options: plain Maven with spring-context, Spring Initializr with Spring Boot starters, Gradle, or an IDE wizard. Configuration options: Java config, component scan, property files (@PropertySource), profiles, environment variables and command-line arguments.
codeExamples:
<dependencies>
  <dependency><groupId>org.springframework</groupId><artifactId>spring-context</artifactId><version>6.1.5</version></dependency>
  <dependency><groupId>org.slf4j</groupId><artifactId>slf4j-simple</artifactId><version>2.0.12</version></dependency>
</dependencies>
mvn -q compile exec:java -Dexec.mainClass=com.shop.App

// OUTPUT:
// order placed: A1 x2

expert.content:
The class Attribute Must Be the Fully Qualified Name

The most common first-run failure in this example is a mismatch between the package in the Java file and the package written in the XML. The bean class is declared as com.test.Student, so the Java file must begin with package com.test;. Change one and not the other and you get:

org.springframework.beans.factory.CannotLoadBeanClassException:
  Cannot find class [com.velocity.Student] for bean with name 's'
  defined in class path resource [spring.xml];
  nested exception is java.lang.ClassNotFoundException: com.velocity.Student

The second most common is putting spring.xml in src/main/java instead of src/main/resources, which produces:

java.io.FileNotFoundException: class path resource [spring.xml]
  cannot be opened because it does not exist

Both messages name the exact cause. Read the class name and the resource name in the stack trace before changing anything.

getBean() by Name vs by Type

getBean("s") returns Object and forces a cast, so a typo in the id is only discovered at runtime, and a wrong cast throws ClassCastException. Every modern overload takes the type as well.

Close the Context - or Lose the Destroy Callbacks

A container holds singletons and their resources. If the program ends without closing it, @PreDestroy and destroy-method never run: connection pools are not drained, files are not flushed.

ClassPathXmlApplicationContext implements AutoCloseable, so try-with-resources is the tidy form.

The Same Application Without XML

The XML version is the clearest way to see what the container does. This is the identical application written the way current projects write it - useful to compare side by side, because every XML element has a direct counterpart.

XML formAnnotation / Java-config form
<bean id="s" class="...">@Component on the class, or a @Bean method
<property name="city" value="pune"/>@Value("pune") on the field, or a setter call inside @Bean
<context:component-scan base-package="com.test"/>@ComponentScan("com.test")
new ClassPathXmlApplicationContext("spring.xml")new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(AppConfig.class)

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What three things does a minimal Spring application need?A bean class (POJO), a configuration file declaring the bean, and a main class that creates the container and calls getBean().
Where must spring.xml be placed and why?src/main/resources. Maven copies that folder onto the classpath, which is where ClassPathResource looks.
What does the id attribute of a bean do?Names the bean so getBean("id") can find it, and so other beans can reference it with ref="id".
What does <property> do internally?Spring calls the matching setter - <property name="city"> calls setCity(). Without that setter, injection fails.
What is Maven and why use it here?A POM-based build tool that downloads dependencies from a central repository into your local one, so you never match jar versions by hand.
Difference between groupId and artifactId?groupId is the organisation/project group id, unique across the organisation; artifactId is the project name.
Difference between spring-core and spring-context?spring-core carries the BeanFactory and the base IoC machinery; spring-context builds ApplicationContext on it, adding events, i18n, scheduling and annotation config.
Why prefer getBean(Student.class) over getBean("s")?No cast, and a wrong name becomes a compile error rather than a runtime NoSuchBeanDefinitionException.
What happens if you never close the context?Destroy callbacks (@PreDestroy, destroy-method) never run, so pooled resources are not released.
Bean class in XML does not match the package - what error?CannotLoadBeanClassException wrapping a ClassNotFoundException that names the class it could not find.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Use constructor injection to give a bean its collaborators.
  • Externalize values with @Value("${app.name}") and property sources.
  • Log with SLF4J instead of System.out in real applications.

Senior Notes

  • Prefer Spring Boot for new applications; plain Spring Core is useful to understand the container.
  • Keep configuration classes small and explicit; avoid broad component scans of third-party packages.
  • Write a test with @SpringJUnitConfig to verify the context starts and beans wire up.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: missing the component scan (no beans found: NoSuchBeanDefinitionException), a wrong package in @ComponentScan, forgetting to close the context (destroy callbacks not run), and mixing XML and annotations without reason. Close the context with try-with-resources.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Keep startup light: scan only your packages, avoid heavy work in constructors, and use @PostConstruct or lazy beans for expensive initialization. Measure with simple timestamps or Actuator when you move to Boot.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: the same code runs in tests, a command-line job and a web app because the wiring lives in configuration, not in the classes. A scheduled batch can reuse the services unchanged.

topics.name: Dependency Injection (Setter & Constructor)

beginner.content:
What is Dependency Injection?

The process of passing the required input from the configuration file into the Spring bean class is called Dependency Injection.

There are two types:

TypeHow it works
Setter-based injectionThe container calls the bean's setter methods to supply each value. Declared with <property>.
Constructor-based injectionThe container calls a parameterised constructor and supplies the values as arguments. Declared with <constructor-arg>.

The Spring container knows which one to perform by reading the configuration file - <property> means setter injection, <constructor-arg> means constructor injection.

1. Setter-Based Injection

• Achieved through setter methods.
• The container uses the setter in the dependent class to inject its dependencies - primitive values or any other type.
• The class must contain a setter for each injected property. Without it the container cannot inject the dependency.

Steps

1. Create the new project   2. Create the Spring bean class   3. Add the Maven dependencies   4. Create the test class   5. Create spring.xml   6. Run   7. Check output

Step 1 - Create the Project

File -> New -> Other -> type Maven Project -> Next -> tick Create a simple project -> Next. Enter injection as Group Id and DependancyInjectionSetter as Artifact Id, then Finish.

Step 2 - Create the Spring Bean Class

Note that Student has a setter for city but no getter. Setter injection needs only the setter.
codeExamples:
<!-- Step 3 - Maven dependencies in pom.xml -->
<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-core</artifactId>
        <version>${spring.version}</version>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-context</artifactId>
        <version>${spring.version}</version>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

<properties>
    <spring.version>3.2.3.RELEASE</spring.version>
</properties>

beginner.content:
Steps 4 and 5 - The Test Class and spring.xml

<property name="city" value="pune"/> tells the container to call setCity("pune") after creating the object.
codeExamples:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<beans xmlns="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans"
       xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
       xsi:schemaLocation="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans
                           http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans/spring-beans.xsd">

    <bean id="s" class="com.velocity.Student">
        <property name="city" value="pune" />
    </bean>

</beans>

beginner.content:
2. Constructor-Based Injection

• Achieved through a parameterised constructor.
• The container uses that constructor to create the bean and assign its properties in one step.

Here Student has three fields and one constructor taking all three. There are no setters at all - and none are needed.
codeExamples:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<beans xmlns="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans"
       xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
       xsi:schemaLocation="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans
                           http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans/spring-beans.xsd">

    <bean id="s" class="com.velocity.Student">
        <constructor-arg value="ashok"></constructor-arg>
        <constructor-arg value="25"></constructor-arg>
        <constructor-arg value="pune"></constructor-arg>
    </bean>

</beans>

// OUTPUT:
Student [name=ashok, age=25, city=pune]

beginner.content:
Why does index come into the picture?

Constructor arguments are matched by position. Change the order in the XML and the values land in the wrong fields:

<constructor-arg value="25"/>      ->  goes into  name
<constructor-arg value="ashok"/>   ->  goes into  age
<constructor-arg value="pune"/>    ->  goes into  city

Result: Student [name=25, age=ashok, city=pune]   -- wrong

All three parameters are String, so the container cannot tell them apart by type and simply takes them in order. To remove the ambiguity, add an explicit index to each argument. Then the XML order stops mattering.
codeExamples:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<beans xmlns="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans"
       xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
       xsi:schemaLocation="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans
                           http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans/spring-beans.xsd">

    <bean id="s" class="com.velocity.Student">
        <constructor-arg value="25"    index="1"></constructor-arg>
        <constructor-arg value="pune"  index="2"></constructor-arg>
        <constructor-arg value="ashok" index="0"></constructor-arg>
    </bean>

</beans>
<!-- OUTPUT: -->
<!-- Student [name=ashok, age=25, city=pune] -->
<!-- The elements are deliberately out of order, and index puts each -->
<!-- value in the right constructor parameter anyway. -->

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Dependency injection gives a bean its dependencies from outside. The two main styles are constructor injection and setter injection.
  • Constructor injection is preferred for required dependencies; setter injection for optional ones.
  • With a single constructor Spring injects it automatically; @Autowired is not needed.

Worked Example 1

Unit test without Spring.

Worked Example 2

Lazy optional lookup.

Practice Exercise 1

Constructor and setter injection.

Practice Exercise 2

Choosing among implementations.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Constructor injection happens during bean instantiation: Spring resolves each constructor parameter by type (and qualifier), creating those beans first. This makes dependencies part of the object's valid state and lets fields be final. Setter and field injection happen after instantiation by reflection, so the object exists in a partially initialized state in between.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Resolution rules: by type, then @Primary, then @Qualifier or @Resource(name), then parameter name. Collections inject all matching beans (ordered by @Order). @Lookup methods and ObjectProvider create prototype instances on demand. @DependsOn controls initialization order.

expert.content:
Three Ways to Disambiguate Constructor Arguments

index is the one the example uses, and it is not the only one. All three exist because positional matching is fragile.

AttributeWhat it matches on
index="0"Parameter position, zero-based. Always works, but a reordered constructor silently breaks it.
type="int"Parameter type. Useless when several parameters share a type - which is exactly the case above.
name="city"Parameter name. The clearest of the three, and survives reordering - but the class must be compiled with debug symbols (-parameters or -g) or carry @ConstructorProperties.
codeExamples:
<!-- name= is the most readable form, and it does not care about order -->
<bean id="s" class="com.velocity.Student">
    <constructor-arg name="city"  value="pune"/>
    <constructor-arg name="name"  value="ashok"/>
    <constructor-arg name="age"   value="25"/>
</bean>
<!-- OUTPUT: -->
<!-- Student [name=ashok, age=25, city=pune] -->
<!-- Requires javac -parameters (Maven: maven.compiler.parameters=true), -->
<!-- otherwise Spring cannot read the parameter names and falls back to -->
<!-- position, which reintroduces the very bug index was added to fix. -->

expert.content:
Setter vs Constructor Injection - Which to Use

AspectSetter injectionConstructor injection
XML element<property><constructor-arg>
Object validityThe object exists briefly in a half-built state before the setters runThe object is fully valid the instant the constructor returns
ImmutabilityFields cannot be final - a setter must be able to write themFields can be final, so the bean is immutable and thread-safe
Optional dependenciesNatural - just do not declare the propertyAwkward - every argument must be supplied
Circular dependency A -> B -> AResolved by Spring for singletonsFails at startup with BeanCurrentlyInCreationException
Partial injectionPossible, and often accidentalImpossible by construction
OverridingA later setter call can overwrite an injected valueCannot be overridden after creation

The Spring team's own recommendation is constructor injection for mandatory dependencies and setter injection for genuinely optional ones. The reason is not style: a class whose constructor takes eight arguments looks like it does too much, and that pressure is useful design feedback. Field injection hides the same eight dependencies and removes the signal.

Injecting Beans, Not Just Values

Everything above injects Strings. The same two mechanisms inject other beans: use ref instead of value.
codeExamples:
<!-- Setter injection of a collaborating bean -->
<bean id="address" class="com.velocity.Address">
    <property name="pincode" value="411001"/>
</bean>

<bean id="employee" class="com.velocity.Employee">
    <property name="balance" value="8000"/>
    <property name="address" ref="address"/>   <!-- ref, not value -->
</bean>

<!-- Constructor injection of the same collaborator -->
<bean id="employee2" class="com.velocity.Employee">
    <constructor-arg value="8000"/>
    <constructor-arg ref="address"/>
</bean>
<!-- OUTPUT: -->
<!-- employee.getAddress().getPincode() returns 411001 -->
<!-- value= is for literals; ref= points at another bean's id. -->

<!-- Collections can be injected too -->
<bean id="course" class="com.velocity.Course">

    <property name="topics">
        <list>
            <value>Spring Core</value>
            <value>Spring MVC</value>
            <value>Spring Boot</value>
        </list>
    </property>

    <property name="fees">
        <map>
            <entry key="regular" value="15000"/>
            <entry key="weekend" value="18000"/>
        </map>
    </property>

    <property name="tutors">
        <list>
            <ref bean="tutorA"/>
            <ref bean="tutorB"/>
        </list>
    </property>
</bean>
<!-- OUTPUT: -->
<!-- topics = [Spring Core, Spring MVC, Spring Boot] -->
<!-- fees   = {regular=15000, weekend=18000} -->

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is dependency injection?Passing the required input into a bean from outside - from the configuration file or the container - rather than the bean creating it itself.
Which two types does Spring support?Setter-based (<property>) and constructor-based (<constructor-arg>).
How does the container decide which one to use?By the configuration: a <property> element triggers the setter, a <constructor-arg> element triggers the constructor.
What must the class provide for setter injection?A public setter for every injected property. Without it, the container cannot inject and startup fails.
Why is index needed on constructor-arg?Arguments are matched by position, so reordering the XML puts values in the wrong parameters - and when several parameters share a type, Spring cannot detect the mistake. index pins each value to a parameter.
Alternatives to index?type (useless with duplicate types) and name (clearest, but needs -parameters at compile time).
Difference between value and ref?value injects a literal converted to the target type; ref injects another bean by its id.
Which injection does Spring recommend, and why?Constructor injection for mandatory dependencies: the object is never half-built, fields can be final, and a long parameter list exposes a class that is doing too much.
Which injection tolerates circular dependencies?Setter/field injection - Spring can patch the cycle after construction. Constructor injection fails fast with BeanCurrentlyInCreationException.
Do you still need @Autowired on a constructor?Not since Spring 4.3, if the class has exactly one constructor. With two or more, one must be annotated.
Can setter injection make a field final?No - a setter must be able to assign it. That is a real advantage of constructor injection.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Field injection (@Autowired on a field) works but hides dependencies and complicates tests; avoid it.
  • Use @Qualifier or @Primary when several beans of the same type exist.
  • Collections and maps of beans can be injected: List<Plugin>.

Senior Notes

  • Circular dependencies are a design smell; fix by redesigning, or use setter injection or @Lazy as a last resort.
  • Inject interfaces, not implementations, to keep coupling low.
  • ObjectProvider<T> supports optional and lazy lookups.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: field injection with private fields in classes you also construct manually (null fields), circular constructor dependencies (BeanCurrentlyInCreationException), huge constructors (a sign the class has too many responsibilities), and injecting concrete classes. Split the class, depend on interfaces and break cycles.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Injection cost is paid once at startup. The practical performance concern is prototype beans created per call and proxies created for AOP and transactions; keep hot paths free of unnecessary proxies and reflection by keeping logic in plain methods.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: plugin architecture. New payment methods are added by creating a new bean; the checkout service receives all of them and selects one by key, with no changes to existing code.

topics.name: Autowiring

beginner.content:
What is Autowiring?

Autowiring is the Spring feature that lets the container inject object dependencies automatically, without you naming them in the configuration file.

Why?

Suppose Employee depends on Address. Without autowiring you wire the reference by hand:

<bean id="a" class="com.velocity.Address">
    <property name="pincode" value="123456"/>
</bean>

<bean id="e" class="com.velocity.Employee">
    <property name="balance" value="8000"/>
    <property name="address" ref="a"/>      <-- written by hand
</bean>

That ref="a" is the line autowiring removes. The container works out for itself which bean fits, creates it, and injects it - so the same work gets done with no XML for it.

PointDetail
AdvantageLess code - the wiring lines disappear from the configuration file.
DisadvantageAutowiring cannot be applied to primitive data types. Only secondary (reference) types can be injected.
Injection styleYou can autowire through either the setter method or the constructor.

The Two Ways to Autowire

ApproachMeaning
XML basedThe autowire attribute on a <bean> element. Four modes: byType, byName, constructor, autodetect.
Annotation based@Autowired on a field, setter or constructor. No XML wiring at all.

The four XML modes

ModeHow the match is made
byTypeThe data type of the property must match the class of a bean declared in the configuration file. Uses setter injection internally.
byNameThe name of the property must match the id/name of a bean in the configuration file. Uses setter injection internally.
constructorMatches constructor parameters by type. Uses constructor injection.
autodetectTries constructor first, and falls back to byType. Uses both styles.

1. byType

• The data type of the attribute must be the same as the data type of a bean defined in the configuration file.
• It uses setter-based injection internally, so the setter must exist.

Steps

1. Create the Maven project   2. Add the Spring dependencies   3. Create the bean classes   4. Create spring.xml   5. Create the test class   6. Run the application

The two bean classes are the same in every example below: Policy holds the plan details, and Categories holds a Policy.
codeExamples:
<!-- Step 2 - pom.xml -->
<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-core</artifactId>
        <version>${spring.version}</version>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-context</artifactId>
        <version>${spring.version}</version>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

<properties>
    <spring.version>4.2.3.RELEASE</spring.version>
</properties>

<!-- Step 4 - spring.xml -->
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<beans xmlns="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans"
       xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
       xsi:schemaLocation="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans
                           http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans/spring-beans.xsd">

    <bean id="categories" class="com.spring.auto.Categories" autowire="byType">
        <property name="name" value="Life Insurance" />
        <!-- no <property name="policy" ref="..."/> -- autowiring supplies it -->
    </bean>

    <bean id="policy" class="com.spring.auto.Policy">
        <property name="planName" value="Term Plan" />
        <property name="planAmount" value="8500" />
    </bean>

</beans>

beginner.content:
byType - Program Explanation

1. The BeanFactory object is created
       BeanFactory factory = new XmlBeanFactory(resource);
       |
       v
2. The container reads the next line of Test.java
       Categories categories = (Categories) factory.getBean("categories");
       |
       v
3. It goes to spring.xml, finds bean id="categories", and reads autowire="byType"
       <bean id="categories" class="com.spring.auto.Categories" autowire="byType">
       |
       v
4. It scans Categories.java for properties that need injecting and finds
       private Policy policy;
       |
       v
5. It looks through spring.xml for a bean whose CLASS is com.spring.auto.Policy
       <bean id="policy" class="com.spring.auto.Policy">      -- type matches
       |
       v
6. The Policy object is injected into Categories via setPolicy()
       |
       v
7. Control returns to Test.java and categories.show() runs

Note: rename the bean to id="p" and the program still works. byType never looks at the id - only at the class.

2. byName

• The name of the attribute must be the same as the bean id/name in the configuration file.
• It uses setter-based injection internally.

The Java classes are unchanged. Only the autowire value differs.
codeExamples:
<!-- spring.xml -->
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<beans xmlns="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans"
       xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
       xsi:schemaLocation="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans
                           http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans/spring-beans.xsd">

    <bean id="policy" class="com.spring.auto.Policy">
        <property name="planName" value="Term Plan" />
        <property name="planAmount" value="8500" />
    </bean>

    <bean id="categories" class="com.spring.auto.Categories" autowire="byName">
        <property name="name" value="Life Insurance" />
    </bean>

</beans>
<!-- OUTPUT: -->
<!-- Categories name>>Life Insurance -->
<!-- Policy Name>>Term Plan -->
<!-- Policy Amount>>8500 -->

beginner.content:
byName - Program Explanation

The flow is the same as byType up to step 4. The matching step is what changes:

4. Container finds the property in Categories.java
       private Policy policy;          -- property NAME is "policy"
       |
       v
5. It looks for a bean whose ID is exactly "policy"
       <bean id="policy" class="com.spring.auto.Policy">   -- name matches
       |
       v
6. setPolicy() is called with that bean

Note: with byName the bean id in spring.xml and the field name in Categories.java must be identical. Rename the bean to id="p" and the field is silently left null - show() then throws a NullPointerException on policy.getPlanName(). This is the opposite of byType, where the id is irrelevant.

3. constructor

This mode uses constructor-based injection: the container matches the constructor parameters by type. Both classes now have parameterised constructors instead of setters.
codeExamples:
<!-- spring.xml -->
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<beans xmlns="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans"
       xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
       xsi:schemaLocation="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans
                           http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans/spring-beans.xsd">

    <bean id="categories" class="com.spring.auto.Categories" autowire="constructor">
        <constructor-arg value="Life Insurance"></constructor-arg>
        <!-- the Policy argument is supplied by autowiring, by type -->
    </bean>

    <bean id="policy" class="com.spring.auto.Policy">
        <constructor-arg value="Term Plan"></constructor-arg>
        <constructor-arg value="8500"></constructor-arg>
    </bean>

</beans>
<!-- OUTPUT: -->
<!-- Categories name>>Life Insurance -->
<!-- Policy Name>>Term Plan -->
<!-- Policy Amount>>8500 -->

beginner.content:
4. autodetect

It uses both styles: the container looks for a suitable parameterised constructor first, and if the bean has none it falls back to byType with setters. The classes here are the setter-based versions from the byType example.

Note: with the constructor mode and with autodetect, the bean id and the field name do not have to match - matching is by type. Only byName requires them to be the same.
codeExamples:
<!-- spring.xml -->
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<beans xmlns="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans"
       xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
       xsi:schemaLocation="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans
                           http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans/spring-beans.xsd">

    <bean id="categories" class="com.spring.auto.Categories" autowire="autodetect">
        <property name="name" value="Life Insurance" />
    </bean>

    <bean id="policy" class="com.spring.auto.Policy">
        <property name="planName" value="Term Plan" />
        <property name="planAmount" value="8500" />
    </bean>

</beans>
<!-- OUTPUT: -->
<!-- Categories name>>Life Insurance -->
<!-- Policy Name>>Term Plan -->
<!-- Policy Amount>>8500 -->
<!-- Categories has no parameterised constructor, so autodetect -->
<!-- fell back to byType and used setPolicy(). -->

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Autowiring tells Spring to find and inject matching beans automatically. Use @Autowired on constructors, setters or fields.
  • Matching is by type first; if several candidates exist, Spring uses @Primary, @Qualifier or the parameter name.
  • If no bean matches a required dependency, the context fails to start with a clear error.

Worked Example 1

Ambiguity error.

Worked Example 2

Autowire by generic type.

Practice Exercise 1

Strategy via Map injection.

Practice Exercise 2

Optional dependency.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Autowiring is implemented by AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor. For each bean it finds injection points (constructors, methods, fields), asks the BeanFactory to resolve a dependency descriptor (type, generics, qualifiers, required flag) and injects the result. Candidate selection narrows from all beans of the type to one using primary, qualifier and name rules.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Controls: @Primary, @Qualifier (also custom qualifier annotations), @Resource(name=...), @Value, @Lazy on an injection point (injects a proxy resolved on first use), generics matching, and @Order/Ordered for lists.

expert.content:
The Four Modes Side by Side

AspectbyTypebyNameconstructor
Matches onProperty type vs bean classProperty name vs bean idConstructor parameter type
Injection usedSetterSetterConstructor
Setter required?YesYesNo
Bean id must match field name?NoYesNo
Two candidate beans of the typeStartup fails - ambiguousFine - the id decidesStartup fails - ambiguous
No candidate foundField left null, silentlyField left null, silentlyStartup fails

That last row is the one that bites. XML autowiring by type or name is silent on failure: no matching bean simply means the property is never set, and you find out with a NullPointerException the first time the field is used. Set dependency-check (Spring 2.x) or, far better, use @Autowired, which is required by default and fails at startup with a message naming the missing bean.
codeExamples:
<!-- byType with two Policy beans -->
<bean id="term"     class="com.spring.auto.Policy"/>
<bean id="endowment" class="com.spring.auto.Policy"/>

<bean id="categories" class="com.spring.auto.Categories" autowire="byType"/>
<!-- OUTPUT at startup: -->
<!-- UnsatisfiedDependencyException: -->
<!--   expected single matching bean but found 2: term,endowment -->

<!-- byName has no such problem - the field name "policy" picks exactly one -->
<bean id="policy" class="com.spring.auto.Policy"/>

expert.content:
autowire="autodetect" Is Gone

autodetect was deprecated in Spring 3.0 and removed in Spring 4.0, along with dependency-check. It is shown above because it appears in course material and in pre-4.0 projects, but a Spring 4+ container rejects it:

org.xml.sax.SAXParseException: cvc-enumeration-valid: Value 'autodetect'
  is not facet-valid with respect to enumeration
  '[default, no, byName, byType, constructor]'

The reason it was dropped is the reason it was always risky: "constructor if there is one, otherwise byType" means adding a constructor to a class silently changes how it is wired. Explicit is better. In new code, use @Autowired on a constructor and be done.

Annotation-Based Autowiring - What You Will Actually Write

XML autowiring is worth understanding because it names the matching rules precisely. Real projects use annotations, and the rules carry straight over: @Autowired matches by type, exactly like byType, and falls back to the field or parameter name when two candidates tie - which is byName acting as the tie-breaker.

AnnotationPurpose
@AutowiredSpring's own. Injects by type; required = false makes the dependency optional.
@Qualifier("name")Names the bean to use when several match by type. This is the fix for the ambiguity error.
@PrimaryOn the bean class. Marks one candidate as the default, so injection points need no @Qualifier.
@Resource(name="...")JSR-250. Matches by name first, then by type - effectively byName.
@InjectJSR-330. Behaves like @Autowired but has no required attribute.

To make annotations work in an XML project, add <context:annotation-config/> or <context:component-scan base-package="com.spring.auto"/>. Spring Boot does this for you.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is autowiring?Letting the container inject object dependencies automatically instead of naming them with ref in the configuration file.
What are the XML autowire modes?no (default), byName, byType, constructor - plus autodetect, which existed until Spring 4.0.
Can autowiring inject primitives?No. Only secondary/reference types. Primitives and Strings must be set with value.
Difference between byType and byName?byType matches the property's type against a bean's class and ignores ids; byName matches the property's name against a bean id and ignores types.
With byName, must the bean id equal the field name?Yes. If it does not, the property is silently left null and you get a NullPointerException on first use.
What happens with byType if two beans of the type exist?Startup fails with "expected single matching bean but found 2". Fix it with @Qualifier, @Primary, or by switching to byName.
What does autowire="constructor" do?Matches constructor parameters by type and uses constructor injection, so no setters are needed.
Is autodetect still available?No - deprecated in Spring 3.0, removed in 4.0, because adding a constructor to a class silently changed how it was wired.
Does @Autowired match by type or by name?By type first; the field or parameter name is used only to break a tie between equally valid candidates.
@Autowired vs @Resource?@Autowired (Spring) is by type with name as tie-breaker; @Resource (JSR-250) is by name first, then by type.
How do you make an autowired dependency optional?@Autowired(required = false), or declare the field as Optional<T> or ObjectProvider<T>.
What is the main risk of XML autowiring?It fails silently: no matching bean means the property is simply never set, and the error surfaces much later as a NullPointerException.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Modes in XML: byType, byName, constructor, no. With annotations, constructor injection with one constructor is automatic.
  • @Autowired(required = false) or Optional<T> makes a dependency optional.
  • @Resource and @Inject are standard alternatives.

Senior Notes

  • Prefer constructor autowiring; it works with final fields and plain unit tests.
  • Many candidates: inject Map<String, T> to select by bean name at runtime (strategy pattern).
  • Be careful with generics: Spring can autowire by generic type (Repository<Order>) when types are resolvable.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: ambiguous candidates, autowiring a concrete class that is wrapped in a JDK proxy (type mismatch), relying on parameter names (not available without -parameters), and overusing @Lazy to hide circular design problems. Inject interfaces and be explicit with qualifiers.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Resolution cost is only at startup. Runtime cost appears with lazy proxies and scoped proxies, which add an indirection per call; use them only where needed (request-scoped beans in singletons).

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: feature toggles and environment-specific beans. A conditional bean chooses the implementation at startup, and services depend only on the interface.

topics.name: Introduction, Architecture, Modules and Spring Framework vs Spring Boot

beginner.content:
What is the Spring Framework?

• Spring is the most widely used Java application framework. Its core idea is Inversion of Control: instead of your code creating and connecting its dependencies, the Spring container creates the objects (beans), wires them together (dependency injection) and manages their lifecycle. On top of the container Spring provides infrastructure: AOP, transactions, data access, web MVC/WebFlux, security, messaging, testing, caching, scheduling.
• Why it exists: plain Java EE (J2EE) was heavyweight; Spring offered POJO-based programming, loose coupling, easy testing and consistent abstractions (transactions, data access exceptions) over many technologies.
• Today you start with Spring Boot, which auto-configures Spring Framework; but Boot is "Spring with defaults": every Boot behaviour is Spring Core underneath.

intermediate.content:
Spring architecture and modules

LayerModulesPurpose
Core Containerspring-core, spring-beans, spring-context, spring-expression (SpEL)IoC/DI container, resources, events, i18n, SpEL
AOP and instrumentationspring-aop, spring-aspects (AspectJ)Proxies, aspects, cross-cutting concerns
Data access / integrationspring-jdbc, spring-tx, spring-orm, spring-jms, spring-oxmJDBC templates, transactions, ORM integration, messaging
Webspring-web, spring-webmvc, spring-webflux, spring-websocketMVC, REST, reactive web, WebSocket
Testspring-testTestContext framework, MockMvc, JUnit 5 integration
• Related projects: Spring Boot, Spring Data, Spring Security, Spring Cloud, Spring Batch, Spring Integration. Each depends on Spring Framework's core container.
• Spring Core (the container) = spring-core + spring-beans + spring-context (+ spring-expression and spring-aop). In this course "Spring Core" also covers transactions, JDBC, validation, events, AOP and testing.

expert.content:
Spring Framework vs Spring Boot

Spring FrameworkSpring Boot
PurposeThe foundation: container, AOP, transactions, MVC, data accessOpinionated layer that makes Spring applications easy to create and run
ConfigurationYou declare beans (XML/annotations/Java) and infrastructure (view resolvers, transaction manager, data source)Auto-configuration creates sensible beans from the classpath and properties
DependenciesYou choose and align versionsStarters and a managed BOM
ServerDeploy a WAR to an external servlet containerEmbedded Tomcat/Jetty/Undertow/Netty; runnable jar
Production featuresBuild yourselfActuator: health, metrics, info
Entry pointCreate ApplicationContext yourselfSpringApplication.run(...)
• Boot adds no new container: @SpringBootApplication = @Configuration + @EnableAutoConfiguration + @ComponentScan. Auto-configuration classes are ordinary @Configuration classes guarded by @Conditional... annotations. Understanding Spring Core means you can read and override anything Boot does.

interviewQA: What is the Spring Framework?

A Java application framework built around an IoC container that creates and wires beans (dependency injection) and provides infrastructure such as AOP, transactions, data access, web MVC, security integration and testing support.
What is the difference between Spring Framework and Spring Boot?

Spring Framework is the foundation (container, AOP, tx, MVC); Spring Boot adds auto-configuration, starters, embedded servers and production features on top of it, so applications need little setup. Boot does not replace the container.
What are the main Spring modules?
Core Container (core, beans, context, expression), AOP, data access/integration (jdbc, tx, orm, jms), web (web, webmvc, webflux) and test.

topics.name: IoC, Dependency Injection and Why They Matter

beginner.content:
Inversion of Control

• Normally your object controls how it gets its collaborators: this.repo = new JdbcCourseRepository(dataSource). With IoC the control is inverted: a framework (the container) decides which implementation is used and when it is created, and hands it in. Hollywood principle: "don't call us, we'll call you".
• Dependency Injection (DI) is the main IoC technique: a class declares its dependencies (constructor parameters, setters, fields) and the container injects them. Alternatives: Service Locator (the class asks a registry), factories.
• Benefits: loose coupling (depend on interfaces), testability (inject fakes), configurability (swap implementations by config), lifecycle management by the container, and cross-cutting features through proxies.

intermediate.content:
IoC vs DI vs Service Locator

Dependency InjectionService Locator
Who provides dependencies?The container pushes them inThe class pulls them (ctx.getBean(...))
Dependencies visible?Yes, in the constructor signatureHidden inside method bodies
TestingEasy: pass fakesNeeds a configured locator
Coupling to the frameworkNone (POJOs)The class depends on the locator
• In Spring, avoid ApplicationContext.getBean() in application code (it is the Service Locator anti-pattern); use it only at the entry point or in infrastructure code. Prefer ObjectProvider when you need lazy/optional lookups.
• DI makes the object graph an explicit design: the container assembles it from configuration (composition root); business classes only use their collaborators.

expert.content:
What the container does for you

• Reads configuration (annotations, Java config, XML) into bean definitions; instantiates beans in dependency order; resolves and injects dependencies by type/name/qualifier; applies post-processors (property placeholders, @Autowired, validation, AOP proxies); invokes lifecycle callbacks (init/destroy); publishes events; destroys beans on shutdown.
• You design with small cohesive classes and interfaces; the container is the glue. This is why a Spring application can switch a data source, a clock or a payment gateway by changing a bean definition, not business code.

interviewQA: What is Inversion of Control?
A design principle where the framework controls object creation and wiring instead of the application code; the class receives its collaborators rather than creating them.
What is Dependency Injection?
A form of IoC in which an object declares its dependencies and the container injects them through constructors, setters or fields, giving loose coupling and easy testing.
Why is calling getBean() in application code discouraged?
It is the Service Locator anti-pattern: dependencies become hidden, the class depends on the container and testing gets harder. Use constructor injection or ObjectProvider.

topics.name: Core Container: BeanFactory, ApplicationContext and Configuration Metadata

beginner.content:
BeanFactory

• BeanFactory is the root interface of the IoC container: getBean(name|type), containsBean, isSingleton, getType. The main implementation is DefaultListableBeanFactory. It provides dependency injection and bean lifecycle and lazily instantiates beans (on first getBean), but offers no enterprise features by itself.
• Use directly only in constrained environments; applications use ApplicationContext.

intermediate.content:
ApplicationContext

• ApplicationContext extends BeanFactory and adds enterprise features: eager singleton instantiation at startup (errors fail fast), automatic registration of post-processors (BPP/BFPP), event publication (ApplicationEventPublisher), message source / i18n (MessageSource), resource loading (ResourcePatternResolver), Environment (profiles/properties), annotation processing, AOP integration, parent/child contexts, lifecycle (refresh, close).
• Implementations: ClassPathXmlApplicationContext, FileSystemXmlApplicationContext, AnnotationConfigApplicationContext (plain Java apps), AnnotationConfigServletWebServerApplicationContext (Boot servlet apps), GenericApplicationContext, AnnotationConfigWebApplicationContext/XmlWebApplicationContext (legacy web).

expert.content:
BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext, and configuration metadata

BeanFactoryApplicationContext

Post-processorsMust be registered manuallyDetected and applied automatically
Events, i18n, resourcesNoYes
Annotation support (@Autowired, @PostConstruct)Only if you register the processorsYes (via AnnotationConfigUtils)
UseEmbedded/low-levelApplications
• Configuration metadata tells the container what beans to create and how to wire them: (1) XML (<bean>), (2) annotation-based (@Component + @ComponentScan, @Autowired), (3) Java-based (@Configuration + @Bean), and programmatic registration. All end up as BeanDefinition objects in the registry. They can be mixed; Java/annotation configuration is the modern default.

interviewQA: BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext?

ApplicationContext extends BeanFactory with eager singleton creation, automatic post-processor registration, events, i18n, resource loading and Environment support; BeanFactory is the minimal lazy container. Applications should use ApplicationContext.
What is configuration metadata?
The instructions (XML, annotations, Java @Configuration) that describe beans and wiring; the container turns them into BeanDefinition objects and creates beans from them.
Which ApplicationContext implementation is used in a Spring Boot web app?
AnnotationConfigServletWebServerApplicationContext (or the reactive/ non-web variants for other application types), created by SpringApplication.

topics.name: Constructor, Setter and Field Injection: Comparison and Best Practices

beginner.content:
The three injection styles

• Constructor injection: dependencies are constructor parameters. Since Spring 4.3 a class with one constructor needs no @Autowired. Setter injection: @Autowired on a setter, for optional/changeable dependencies. Field injection: @Autowired directly on a private field (reflection).

Constructor vs setter vs field injection

expert.content:
Best practices for DI

• Prefer constructor injection with final fields (Lombok @RequiredArgsConstructor reduces noise). Keep constructors with few parameters (more than 4-5 means the class has too many responsibilities: split it).
• Program to interfaces; inject the interface, not the implementation. Avoid injecting the ApplicationContext. Do not use static access to beans. Never use new for collaborators that should be beans (it bypasses the container, so no AOP/transactions).
• Avoid circular dependencies by redesign (extract a third bean, use events). Keep business logic out of configuration classes. Use @Qualifier/@Primary deliberately when several candidates exist. Inject values through @Value/@ConfigurationProperties, not by reading system properties in code. Prefer small, stateless singleton beans.

interviewQA: Constructor vs setter vs field injection?

Constructor injection guarantees required dependencies, allows final fields and easy unit tests and exposes class bloat; setter injection suits optional dependencies; field injection is concise but hides dependencies, prevents immutability and complicates testing, so it is discouraged.
Do you need @Autowired on a constructor?
Not when the class has a single constructor (Spring 4.3+); with several constructors mark the one to use with @Autowired.
Why is field injection discouraged?
You cannot create the object correctly without reflection or Spring, dependencies are hidden and mutable, and circular dependencies go undetected.

topics.name: Autowiring, @Autowired, @Qualifier, @Primary, @Resource, @Inject and Dependency Resolution

beginner.content:
Autowiring and @Autowired

• Autowiring lets Spring resolve dependencies automatically. With annotations (@Autowired) the default mode is by type: Spring finds the bean assignable to the parameter type. If exactly one candidate exists it is injected; none → NoSuchBeanDefinitionException (unless optional); several → NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException unless disambiguated.
• @Autowired works on constructors, setters, fields and methods; collections/maps inject all beans of a type (List<PaymentProcessor>, Map<String, PaymentProcessor> keyed by bean name); processed by AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor. XML modes: no, byName, byType, constructor.

intermediate.content:
@Qualifier, @Primary and name-based resolution

• Several candidates of one type need disambiguation. @Primary marks the default candidate (on the bean class or @Bean method). @Qualifier("name") at the injection point chooses a specific bean (by bean name or by qualifier label on the bean). @Qualifier wins over @Primary.
• Resolution order for an injection point: (1) candidates by type (including generics); (2) if several: @Qualifier; (3) @Primary; (4) highest @Priority (jakarta.annotation.Priority); (5) fall back to matching the parameter/field name to a bean name (works if compiled with -parameters, default in Boot/Maven plugin). Otherwise an exception.
• Custom qualifier annotations (meta-annotated with @Qualifier) give typed, refactoring-safe labels.

expert.content:
@Resource, @Inject and dependency resolution

• Prefer @Autowired (or implicit constructor injection) in Spring code; @Inject keeps code container-neutral (jakarta.inject dependency); @Resource is handy for name-based lookup of a specific bean. Processed by AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor and CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor.
• Debugging dependency resolution: read the exception (it lists candidates), enable logging.level.org.springframework.beans=DEBUG, inspect ctx.getBeanNamesForType(X.class), check scanning packages and profiles/conditions.

interviewQA: @Autowired vs @Qualifier vs @Primary?
@Autowired injects by type; when several beans match, @Primary marks the default candidate and @Qualifier at the injection point selects a specific one, overriding @Primary.
How does Spring resolve a dependency?

It finds candidates by type, then narrows using @Qualifier, @Primary, @Priority and finally the injection point name matching a bean name; zero or ambiguous matches cause an exception unless optional.
@Autowired vs @Resource vs @Inject?
@Autowired is Spring's by-type injection with required/qualifier support; @Inject is the JSR-330 equivalent; @Resource resolves by name first and works on fields and setters but not constructors.

topics.name: Optional Dependencies, Circular Dependencies and Lazy Dependency Resolution

beginner.content:
Optional dependencies

• A mandatory dependency that is missing fails at startup (good: fail fast). For truly optional ones: @Autowired(required = false), a parameter of type Optional<T>, @Nullable, ObjectProvider<T> (getIfAvailable(), getIfUnique(), ifAvailable(...), stream()), or an empty collection injected when no beans exist.

intermediate.content:
Circular dependencies

• A circular dependency: A needs B and B needs A. Constructor injection fails fast: BeanCurrentlyInCreationException (the object cannot be built because each needs the other first). Setter/field injection of singletons used to work through early references (a three-level cache: singleton objects, early singleton objects, singleton factories), hiding the design smell; Spring Boot 2.6+ prohibits circular references by default (spring.main.allow-circular-references=false).
• Fix by design: extract the shared logic into a third bean both depend on, invert one dependency using an interface/event (ApplicationEventPublisher), move behaviour so the dependency flows one way (layers), or merge classes that are really one.
• Workarounds (last resort): @Lazy on one injection point (injects a lazy-resolution proxy), setter injection, ObjectProvider/Provider resolved at call time, @PostConstruct lookups.

expert.content:
Lazy dependency resolution

• @Lazy on a bean definition delays creation until first use (faster startup, but errors appear later); on an injection point it injects a proxy that resolves the real bean on the first method call: useful for breaking cycles, expensive beans, optional features.
• ObjectProvider<T> / jakarta.inject.Provider / ObjectFactory give explicit control: each getObject() call can return a new prototype instance or the current scoped bean, which solves the scoped bean in singleton problem (injecting a prototype or request-scoped bean into a singleton otherwise freezes one instance).
• Global lazy initialisation: spring.main.lazy-initialization=true (Boot) trades startup time for first-request latency and late failures: be careful in production.

interviewQA: What is a circular dependency and how does Spring handle it?

Two or more beans depend on each other. Constructor injection fails with BeanCurrentlyInCreationException; setter/field cycles were once resolved via early references, but Boot 2.6+ forbids them by default. Fix by redesigning (third bean, events) or as a last resort use @Lazy.
What does @Lazy do?
On a bean definition it defers instantiation until first use; on an injection point it injects a lazy-resolution proxy. It is used to speed startup, delay expensive beans and break cycles.
How do you inject a prototype bean into a singleton correctly?
Inject an ObjectProvider/Provider (or use a scoped proxy or lookup method) and call getObject() each time, instead of injecting the prototype directly, which would be created only once.

topics.name: What Is a Bean: Definition, Registration, Instantiation and Naming

beginner.content:
What is a Spring bean?

• A bean is an object that is instantiated, assembled and managed by the Spring IoC container. Any class can be a bean (a POJO); what makes it a bean is that the container created it from a bean definition. Objects you create with new yourself are not beans (no injection, no AOP).
• A BeanDefinition is the recipe: class name, scope, constructor arguments and property values, dependencies (depends-on), lazy flag, init/destroy method names, primary/autowire candidate flags, factory method. The registry (BeanDefinitionRegistry, i.e. the bean factory) stores definitions by bean name.

intermediate.content:
Bean registration, instantiation and naming

• Registration happens through: @Component scanning, @Bean methods in @Configuration classes, @Import (classes, ImportSelector, ImportBeanDefinitionRegistrar), XML <bean>, and programmatic registerBean. Instantiation ways: constructor (default), static factory method, instance factory method (@Bean methods are factory methods), and FactoryBean.
• Naming: scanned components get a default name = decapitalised class name (CourseService → courseService; URLService → URLService); @Bean method name is the bean name; explicit names via @Component("name"), @Bean("name")/name={...} (aliases), or a custom BeanNameGenerator. Names must be unique in a context (overriding is disabled by default in Boot).

expert.content:
Initialisation and destruction at a glance

• After instantiation and dependency injection a bean is initialised (init callbacks, then post-processors such as AOP proxy creation) and is ready for use; at shutdown it is destroyed (destroy callbacks) in reverse dependency order. The full ordered lifecycle is covered in the Bean Lifecycle section.
• Quick summary: constructor → dependencies injected → aware callbacks → BeanPostProcessor.before → @PostConstruct → afterPropertiesSet → custom init → BeanPostProcessor.after (proxies) → ready → @PreDestroy → destroy → custom destroy.
• Singleton beans are created at startup; prototype beans are created on each request and Spring does not call their destroy callbacks (the caller owns them).

interviewQA: What is a Spring bean?
An object instantiated, wired and managed by the Spring IoC container from a bean definition; objects created with new outside the container are not beans.
What is a BeanDefinition?
The metadata describing how to create a bean: class, scope, constructor args/properties, dependencies, lazy flag, init/destroy methods and factory details, stored in the container's registry.
How are default bean names generated?
For scanned stereotypes the simple class name with a lowercase first letter (courseService); for @Bean methods the method name; explicit names can be set in the annotation or via a BeanNameGenerator.

topics.name: Bean Scopes: Singleton, Prototype, Request, Session, Application and Custom

beginner.content:
Singleton and prototype

• singleton (default): one shared instance per container (not per JVM and not the GoF singleton: per bean definition per context). Created eagerly at startup, cached, destroyed on shutdown. Must be thread-safe and stateless (or carefully synchronised): most services, repositories and controllers.
• prototype: a new instance on every request to the container (getBean or injection). Spring creates and wires it but does not manage its destruction (no @PreDestroy). Use for stateful, short-lived objects (builders, command objects).

intermediate.content:
Web scopes: request, session, application (and websocket)

• Available only in a web-aware ApplicationContext: request (one instance per HTTP request), session (per HTTP session: e.g. a shopping cart, user preferences; remember it must be Serializable for clustering), application (per ServletContext, shared by the whole web app: like a singleton but bound to the servlet context), websocket (per WebSocket session). Shortcuts: @RequestScope, @SessionScope, @ApplicationScope.
• Scoped proxies: injecting a request/session bean into a singleton needs a proxy (proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS, which the shortcut annotations set) so each call is delegated to the instance of the current request/session. Without it injection fails (no scope active at startup) or freezes one instance.

expert.content:
Custom bean scopes and the scoped-bean problem

• Implement Scope (get(name, ObjectFactory), remove, registerDestructionCallback, getConversationId) and register with ConfigurableBeanFactory.registerScope("tenant", scope) (or a CustomScopeConfigurer bean). Spring ships SimpleThreadScope (a bean per thread; not registered by default), and Spring Cloud adds refresh. Typical custom scopes: per-tenant, per-thread, per-conversation, per-workflow.
ScopeInstancesDestroy callbacksThread-safety needed?
singleton1 per containerYesYes
prototype1 per request to the containerNoNot shared
