request / session / applicationper request / session / servlet contextYes (request, session)session and application: yes
custom (tenant, thread)as you defineIf you register callbacksDepends
• Singleton depending on a shorter scope: use ObjectProvider, a scoped proxy, or a @Lookup method; never inject the short-lived bean directly without a proxy.

interviewQA: What are the bean scopes in Spring?
singleton (default, one per container), prototype (new per request), and in web contexts request, session, application and websocket; custom scopes can be registered by implementing Scope.
Singleton scope vs the Singleton design pattern?

Spring's singleton means one instance per bean definition per ApplicationContext, not one per JVM or classloader, and it is not enforced by a private constructor; two contexts can each have their own instance.
How do you use a request-scoped bean inside a singleton?
Inject it through a scoped proxy (the @RequestScope annotation does this) or an ObjectProvider, so each call resolves the instance for the current request rather than a single frozen one.

topics.name: Bean Initialisation and Destruction: Hooks and Choosing One

beginner.content:
Initialisation hooks

• Three standard ways to run code after dependency injection: @PostConstruct (Jakarta annotation: preferred, no Spring dependency), InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet() (Spring interface), and a custom init method (@Bean(initMethod = "...") / XML init-method; for third-party classes). They run in that order for the same bean. Use init for validation of required state, opening resources, warming caches, registering with other components.
• Do not use the constructor for work that needs injected collaborators (fields are not yet set unless constructor-injected) or that can fail; keep @PostConstruct fast (it delays startup) and avoid calling transactional/proxied methods of the same bean there (the proxy does not exist yet).

intermediate.content:
Destruction hooks and the shutdown order

• On context close (ctx.close(), a JVM shutdown hook registered by Boot, or SIGTERM): beans are destroyed in reverse dependency order (a bean is destroyed before the beans it depends on). Hooks: @PreDestroy → DisposableBean.destroy() → custom destroy method. Inferred destroy methods: for @Bean methods Spring automatically calls a public no-arg close() or shutdown() if present (disable with destroyMethod = "" when the container must not close a shared resource).
• Prototype beans are never destroyed by Spring; the caller must release resources. Beans may not get destroy callbacks if the JVM is killed (kill -9) or the context is never closed (registerShutdownHook() in plain Java apps).

expert.content:
Choosing between @PostConstruct, InitializingBean and init-method

OptionWhenNotes
@PostConstruct / @PreDestroyYour own classes (default choice)No Spring coupling; needs jakarta.annotation; processed by CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor
InitializingBean / DisposableBeanFramework-style codeCouples the class to Spring
@Bean(initMethod/destroyMethod)Third-party classes you cannot modifyExplicit and visible in config
SmartLifecycleStart/stop ordering, background workers, after all beans are readyPhases and async stop (see lifecycle section)
ApplicationRunner / CommandLineRunner / ApplicationReadyEventWork after the application is fully started (Boot)Run data loaders here, not in @PostConstruct

interviewQA: In what order do initialisation callbacks run?

@PostConstruct, then InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet, then the custom init-method; BeanPostProcessor before/after hooks surround them. Destruction: @PreDestroy, DisposableBean.destroy, custom destroy-method.
Does Spring call @PreDestroy on prototype beans?
No. Spring creates and wires prototype beans but does not manage their destruction; the client code must clean them up.
Why avoid heavy work in @PostConstruct?
It runs during context startup and delays or fails the whole application; for non-essential work use ApplicationReadyEvent, a runner or SmartLifecycle after the context is ready.

topics.name: XML, Annotation-Based and Java-Based Configuration

beginner.content:
The three configuration styles

• XML-based (original): <beans> with <bean id class>, <constructor-arg>, <property>, <import resource>, <context:component-scan>, <context:property-placeholder>. Externalises wiring from code; verbose; still found in legacy systems; loaded with ClassPathXmlApplicationContext.
• Annotation-based: stereotypes (@Component ...) discovered by component scanning, wired with @Autowired/@Value; concise; configuration lives next to the code.
• Java-based (modern, recommended for infrastructure): @Configuration classes with @Bean factory methods; type-safe, refactorable, debuggable, with full Java logic and conditions. Most real apps combine annotation scanning for your classes and Java config for third-party/infrastructure beans.
codeExamples:
<!-- 1. XML: beans.xml -->
<beans xmlns="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans" xmlns:context="http://www.springframework.org/schema/context" ...>
  <context:property-placeholder location="classpath:app.properties"/>
  <bean id="dataSource" class="com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariDataSource">
      <property name="jdbcUrl" value="${db.url}"/>
      <property name="username" value="${db.user}"/>
  </bean>
  <bean id="courseRepository" class="com.jsl.JdbcCourseRepository"><constructor-arg ref="dataSource"/></bean>
  <bean id="courseService" class="com.jsl.CourseService" scope="singleton" init-method="init">
      <constructor-arg ref="courseRepository"/>
  </bean>
</beans>
// new ClassPathXmlApplicationContext("beans.xml");

// 2. Annotation-based
@Repository class JdbcCourseRepository { JdbcCourseRepository(DataSource ds) {} }
@Service class CourseService { CourseService(CourseRepository repo) {} }
// <context:component-scan base-package="com.jsl"/>   or   @ComponentScan("com.jsl")

// 3. Java-based
@Configuration
class InfraConfig {
    @Bean HikariDataSource dataSource(@Value("${db.url}") String url) { var ds = new HikariDataSource(); ds.setJdbcUrl(url); return ds; }
}

intermediate.content:
Comparing the styles

XMLAnnotations (scanning)Java config
Type safety / refactoringNo (strings)YesYes
Separation from codeComplete (change without recompiling)Configuration is in the classesSeparate classes, compiled
Third-party classesYesNo (cannot annotate)Yes
Conditional logicLimited (profiles)@Conditional, @ProfileFull Java + conditions
VerbosityHighLowMedium
Typical use todayLegacy systemsApplication classesInfrastructure, library config
• Mix them: @ImportResource("classpath:legacy-beans.xml") in a Java config pulls XML beans in; <context:annotation-config/> enables annotations in XML.

expert.content:
Choosing and migrating configuration styles

• Recommendation: scan your own application classes (@Service, @Repository), use @Configuration for infrastructure and third-party beans, keep XML only for legacy modules and import it with @ImportResource. Migration path: wrap XML in an @ImportResource, replace beans one by one with annotations or @Bean, then delete the XML. Keep configuration declarative (no business logic in @Configuration classes) and split large configs by concern (WebConfig, DataConfig, SecurityConfig).

interviewQA: XML vs annotation vs Java configuration?

XML is external and verbose (legacy); annotations with component scanning are concise for your own classes; Java @Configuration/@Bean is type-safe and ideal for third-party and infrastructure beans. They can be mixed in one context.
How do you use legacy XML beans in a Java-config application?
Add @ImportResource("classpath:beans.xml") to a @Configuration class so the XML definitions are loaded into the same context.
Which configuration style does Spring Boot prefer?
Java-based @Configuration with annotation scanning and auto-configuration; XML is supported but rarely needed.

topics.name: @Configuration, @Bean, @Component, @ComponentScan, @Import and @ImportResource

beginner.content:
@Configuration and @Bean

• @Configuration marks a class as a source of bean definitions; @Bean methods are factory methods: the return value is registered as a bean named after the method. Parameters are injected by type (so @Bean methods can depend on each other through parameters).
• Full vs lite mode: in a @Configuration class (CGLIB-enhanced) calls between @Bean methods are intercepted so they return the same singleton ("inter-bean references"). In a plain @Component class (lite mode) or with @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false) the calls are ordinary Java calls and create new objects: prefer parameter injection (works in both and is faster at startup).
• @Bean attributes: name, initMethod, destroyMethod; companions @Scope, @Lazy, @Primary, @Qualifier, @Profile, @Conditional, @DependsOn.

intermediate.content:
@Component, @ComponentScan and @Import

• @Component (and stereotypes) marks a class for auto-detection; @ComponentScan(basePackages | basePackageClasses | includeFilters | excludeFilters) tells the container where to scan (in Boot, @SpringBootApplication scans its own package and subpackages: keep the main class in the root package). Prefer basePackageClasses (type-safe).
• @Import registers other configuration: @Configuration classes, plain component classes, ImportSelector (returns class names to import: used by @EnableXxx and Boot's auto-configuration) and ImportBeanDefinitionRegistrar (registers bean definitions programmatically). Custom @EnableXxx annotations are @Import meta-annotations.
• @ImportResource loads XML (or Groovy) bean definitions.

expert.content:
ImportBeanDefinitionRegistrar and meta-annotations

• ImportBeanDefinitionRegistrar.registerBeanDefinitions(metadata, registry) registers definitions imperatively; this is how @EnableJpaRepositories, @MapperScan (MyBatis) and Feign's @EnableFeignClients create beans for every annotated interface. Combine with ClassPathScanningCandidateComponentProvider to scan.
• Meta-annotations: build your own composed annotations (@Service is meta-annotated with @Component); Spring's AnnotatedElementUtils/MergedAnnotations look through meta-annotation layers, so a custom @UseCase annotation can carry @Service + @Transactional.

interviewQA: What is the difference between @Component and @Bean?

@Component marks your own class for auto-detection by scanning (class-level, container instantiates it); @Bean is a method-level factory in a @Configuration class, used for third-party classes or when you need custom construction logic.
What does @Configuration do beyond @Component?
The class is enhanced with CGLIB so calls between @Bean methods are intercepted and return the managed singleton (inter-bean references); with proxyBeanMethods=false this is disabled for speed.
How do @EnableXxx annotations work?
They are meta-annotated with @Import pointing to a configuration class, ImportSelector or ImportBeanDefinitionRegistrar that registers the infrastructure beans.

topics.name: @PropertySource, @Value, Environment, EnvironmentPostProcessor, Externalized and Profile-Based Configuration

beginner.content:
@PropertySource, @Value and Environment

• @PropertySource("classpath:app.properties") adds a properties file to the Environment (repeatable; ignoreResourceNotFound; YAML needs a custom factory in plain Spring: Boot loads YAML natively). @Value("${key:default}") injects a property (resolved by a PropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurer; declare it as a static @Bean in plain Spring; Boot does it for you) and supports SpEL (#{...}). Environment gives programmatic access: getProperty(key, type, default), getRequiredProperty, containsProperty, getActiveProfiles, acceptsProfiles(Profiles.of("dev")).

intermediate.content:
EnvironmentPostProcessor and externalized configuration

• Externalized configuration: the same artifact runs everywhere; environment-specific values come from outside the code: property files, environment variables, system properties (-Dkey=value), command-line args, config servers, Kubernetes ConfigMaps/Secrets. Spring's Environment resolves them through ordered property sources.
• EnvironmentPostProcessor (Spring Boot; registered in META-INF/spring.factories/spring/...imports) runs before the context is refreshed to customise the Environment: add property sources (a database/Vault source), compute derived properties, decrypt values, set default profiles. In plain Spring use an ApplicationContextInitializer or context.getEnvironment().getPropertySources().addFirst(...).

expert.content:
Profile-based configuration (introduction)

• Profiles activate different beans/properties per environment: @Profile("dev") on classes or @Bean methods (expressions: "!prod", "dev | test", "cloud & !local"), activated by spring.profiles.active (SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE), -Dspring.profiles.active=..., environment.setActiveProfiles(...) or @ActiveProfiles in tests; default profile default applies when none is active. Boot adds application-{profile}.properties|yml and profile groups. Covered in depth in the Profiles and Properties section.

interviewQA: How does @Value work?
A BeanPostProcessor resolves placeholders (${key:default}) and SpEL (#{...}) against the Environment property sources and converts the result to the target type before injecting it.
What is an EnvironmentPostProcessor?
A Spring Boot hook that runs before the application context is refreshed and can modify the Environment, for example adding a property source from Vault or computing defaults.
@PropertySource vs Environment?
@PropertySource adds a file to the Environment; the Environment is the abstraction through which all property sources and profiles are accessed (via @Value or programmatically).

topics.name: @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller, @RestController, @ControllerAdvice and Custom Stereotypes

beginner.content:
The stereotype annotations

AnnotationLayerExtra behaviour
@ComponentGenericMarks any managed bean (the base stereotype)
@ServiceBusiness/service layerNo extra behaviour: a semantic marker (documentation, AOP pointcuts)
@RepositoryPersistence layerEnables exception translation: native persistence exceptions (SQLException, Hibernate/JPA) become Spring's DataAccessException hierarchy via PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor
@ControllerWeb layer (MVC)Request handler detected by RequestMappingHandlerMapping; methods return view names
@RestControllerWeb layer (REST)@Controller + @ResponseBody: return values are written as JSON/XML
@ControllerAdvice / @RestControllerAdviceCross-cutting webGlobal @ExceptionHandler, @InitBinder, @ModelAttribute for all (or selected) controllers
@ConfigurationConfigurationSource of @Bean definitions (CGLIB-enhanced)
• All are meta-annotated with @Component, so scanning detects them. Use the most specific one: it documents intent, enables layer-specific processing and helps pointcuts (within(@Service *)).

intermediate.content:
Examples in a layered application

• Typical flow: @RestController (HTTP, validation) → @Service (business rules, transactions) → @Repository (data access). A @RestControllerAdvice converts exceptions to HTTP responses once for the whole application.

expert.content:
@Component vs @Service vs @Repository, and custom stereotypes

• Functionally @Component and @Service are identical; @Repository adds exception translation; @Controller/@RestController are detected as web handlers. Choose by layer. Putting @Component everywhere works but loses intent and layer-specific behaviour.
• Custom stereotypes: compose your own annotation from existing ones to encode architecture rules: @UseCase (= @Service + @Transactional), @DomainService, @Adapter (hexagonal), @ReadModel. Combine with ArchUnit tests to enforce layering (controllers must not use repositories).

interviewQA: @Component vs @Service vs @Repository?

All are stereotypes detected by scanning; @Component is generic, @Service marks business logic (semantic), @Repository marks persistence classes and adds automatic exception translation to DataAccessException.
What does @RestController add over @Controller?
It combines @Controller and @ResponseBody, so handler return values are serialised into the HTTP response body (JSON/XML) instead of resolving a view name.
What is @ControllerAdvice used for?
Global cross-cutting behaviour for controllers: @ExceptionHandler methods converting exceptions to responses, @InitBinder and @ModelAttribute shared by many controllers.

topics.name: Component Scanning Filters, Conditional Bean Registration and Bean Naming Strategies

beginner.content:
Component scanning and filters

• @ComponentScan scans the classpath under the given packages for classes with stereotype annotations. Filters refine it: includeFilters/excludeFilters with FilterType ANNOTATION, ASSIGNABLE_TYPE, ASPECTJ, REGEX, CUSTOM (TypeFilter); useDefaultFilters = false to start from nothing. Use to exclude test configs/legacy classes or to include classes without annotations (all implementors of an interface).
• Boot's @SpringBootApplication includes TypeExcludeFilter and AutoConfigurationExcludeFilter so slice tests and auto-configurations are not scanned accidentally. Scanning cost grows with package size: scope packages narrowly.

intermediate.content:
Conditional bean registration

• @Conditional(Condition.class) registers a bean only if a Condition.matches(context, metadata) returns true (checked at registration time). Built on it: @Profile, and Spring Boot's family: @ConditionalOnClass/OnMissingClass, @ConditionalOnBean/OnMissingBean (back off when the user defines their own bean), @ConditionalOnProperty, @ConditionalOnExpression, @ConditionalOnWebApplication, @ConditionalOnResource, @ConditionalOnCloudPlatform, @ConditionalOnJava. This is exactly how auto-configuration works.
• Order matters for OnBean conditions: they depend on registration order, so use them in auto-configuration classes (processed last) rather than in user config.

expert.content:
Bean naming strategies

• Default scanning names: AnnotationBeanNameGenerator (decapitalised simple class name; explicit value of the stereotype or @Named). Duplicate simple names in different packages conflict (ConflictingBeanDefinitionException): give explicit names, or use a FullyQualifiedAnnotationBeanNameGenerator (@ComponentScan(nameGenerator = ...)). @Bean methods use the method name; use name for aliases.
• Tips: prefer injecting by type and avoid relying on names; when you must refer to names (qualifiers, @DependsOn), use constants; bean overriding (same name registered twice) is disabled by default in Spring Boot 2.1+ (spring.main.allow-bean-definition-overriding).

interviewQA: How does conditional bean registration work?

@Conditional (and @Profile, @ConditionalOnProperty, @ConditionalOnMissingBean ...) attach Condition checks evaluated while bean definitions are registered, so a bean is only created when its condition holds; Boot auto-configuration relies on this.
What happens when two scanned beans have the same simple class name?
They get the same default bean name and cause a ConflictingBeanDefinitionException; give explicit names or use a fully qualified bean name generator.
How can you see why an auto-configuration did or did not apply?
Run with --debug (or enable the conditions report via Actuator /actuator/conditions) to see positive and negative condition matches.

topics.name: Container Implementations, the refresh() Process and Startup Sequence

beginner.content:
Container implementations

• The container is a family of classes: DefaultListableBeanFactory is the real engine (bean definition registry + singleton registry + autowiring); every ApplicationContext delegates to one. AbstractApplicationContext implements the template method refresh().
• Common contexts: AnnotationConfigApplicationContext (Java config, plain apps and tests), ClassPathXmlApplicationContext/FileSystemXmlApplicationContext (XML), GenericApplicationContext (programmatic, used by Boot and native/AOT), AnnotationConfigServletWebServerApplicationContext and AnnotationConfigReactiveWebServerApplicationContext (Boot web apps with embedded server).
• A context is refreshable (refresh() can be called again on XML/Annotation contexts that support it) or generic (refresh exactly once).

intermediate.content:
What refresh() does, step by step

#StepDetail
1prepareRefreshMark active, init property sources, validate required properties
2obtainFreshBeanFactoryCreate the bean factory and load bean definitions (scan, @Bean, XML)
3prepareBeanFactoryClass loader, SpEL resolver, ApplicationContextAwareProcessor, register Environment, resolvable dependencies (BeanFactory, ApplicationContext)
4postProcessBeanFactorySubclass hooks (web scopes)
5invokeBeanFactoryPostProcessorsRun BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessors (ConfigurationClassPostProcessor parses @Configuration, @ComponentScan, @Import) then BeanFactoryPostProcessors (property placeholders)
6registerBeanPostProcessorsInstantiate and register BPPs (@Autowired, @PostConstruct, AOP auto-proxy)
7initMessageSource, initApplicationEventMulticasteri18n and event infrastructure
8onRefreshSubclass hook (Boot creates the embedded web server here)
9registerListenersRegister ApplicationListener beans
10finishBeanFactoryInitializationInstantiate all remaining non-lazy singletons
11finishRefreshStart Lifecycle beans, publish ContextRefreshedEvent
• Read this table when debugging startup problems: a bean that needs a post-processor to be already registered but is created in step 5 gets no proxy/no injection ("not eligible for getting processed by all BeanPostProcessors" warning).

expert.content:
Startup sequence in Spring Boot

• SpringApplication.run: create listeners and Environment (EnvironmentPostProcessors, banner) → create the ApplicationContext → apply ApplicationContextInitializers → load sources → refresh() (auto-configuration imported in step 5, web server started in step 8) → afterRefresh → ApplicationStartedEvent → run ApplicationRunner/CommandLineRunner → ApplicationReadyEvent. Failures publish ApplicationFailedEvent and FailureAnalyzers print the friendly error report.
• Measure startup with ApplicationStartup (BufferingApplicationStartup + Actuator /actuator/startup) to find slow beans.

interviewQA: What happens when an ApplicationContext starts?

refresh() loads bean definitions, runs BeanFactoryPostProcessors, registers BeanPostProcessors, initialises i18n/events, instantiates non-lazy singletons and finally starts Lifecycle beans and publishes ContextRefreshedEvent.
What is DefaultListableBeanFactory?
The core implementation of the bean factory and registry that stores bean definitions and singletons and performs autowiring; application contexts delegate to it.
When does Spring Boot start the embedded web server?
During refresh() in the onRefresh() step of a web application context, before the remaining singletons are finished, then the ready event is published after startup completes.

topics.name: Aware Interfaces, FactoryBean, Method Injection and Programmatic Bean Access

beginner.content:
Aware interfaces

• Aware callbacks give a bean access to container infrastructure: BeanNameAware, BeanFactoryAware, BeanClassLoaderAware, ApplicationContextAware, EnvironmentAware, ResourceLoaderAware, ApplicationEventPublisherAware, MessageSourceAware, EmbeddedValueResolverAware. They run after dependency injection and before @PostConstruct (ApplicationContextAwareProcessor handles most).
• They couple code to Spring, so use them in infrastructure/framework code; in application beans inject the needed type directly (Environment, ApplicationEventPublisher and ApplicationContext are injectable via constructor).

intermediate.content:
FactoryBean

• FactoryBean<T> is a bean that produces another object (getObject(), getObjectType(), isSingleton()). The bean named x yields the product; &x returns the factory itself. Used for complex construction (proxies: ProxyFactoryBean, LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBean, JndiObjectFactoryBean). Distinguish: BeanFactory = the container; FactoryBean = a bean that is a factory.

expert.content:
Method injection (@Lookup) and programmatic access

• Method injection solves singleton → prototype: @Lookup on an abstract/overridable method makes Spring generate a CGLIB subclass that returns a fresh bean on each call (lookup-method in XML); replaced-method / MethodReplacer overrides arbitrary methods.
• Programmatic access: ctx.getBean(name | Class | name+Class), getBeansOfType, getBeansWithAnnotation, getBeanNamesForType, ListableBeanFactory, BeanFactoryUtils, ObjectProvider. Use only in infrastructure (plugins, dispatchers, tests), never as a replacement for injection.

interviewQA: FactoryBean vs BeanFactory?
BeanFactory is the IoC container interface; FactoryBean is a special bean that acts as a factory for another object, so getBean("x") returns its product and getBean("&x") returns the factory.
When would you implement ApplicationContextAware?
Rarely: in framework/infrastructure code needing dynamic bean lookup; application beans should receive their collaborators through injection.
How do you get a new prototype each call inside a singleton?
Use ObjectProvider/Provider, a @Lookup method or a scoped proxy instead of injecting the prototype directly.

topics.name: Parent/Child Contexts, Dependency Resolution Internals, Bean Registry and Lifecycle Management

beginner.content:
Context hierarchy

• A context can have a parent (setParent). Lookups go child → parent (never parent → child): children see the parent's beans, and can override by name. Classic Spring MVC: a root context (services, repositories) with a child DispatcherServlet context (controllers, view resolvers). Spring Cloud bootstrap and Actuator management contexts use the same mechanism. Boot normally uses a single context; use hierarchies via SpringApplicationBuilder.parent(...).child(...).

intermediate.content:
Dependency resolution internals and the bean registry

• Creating a bean (AbstractAutowireCapableBeanFactory.doCreateBean): createBeanInstance (constructor resolution + autowiring by ConstructorResolver), populateBean (property/field injection through InstantiationAwareBeanPostProcessors), initializeBean (aware callbacks, BPP before/after, init methods). Singletons are cached in singletonObjects (three-level caches handle early references).
• Registry types: BeanDefinitionRegistry (register/remove/lookup definitions), SingletonBeanRegistry (register existing singleton objects: registerSingleton), AliasRegistry. DependencyDescriptor describes an injection point (type, generics, annotations) and ContextAnnotationAutowireCandidateResolver decides candidates, handling @Qualifier, @Lazy.
• depends-on (@DependsOn) forces ordering when there is no direct dependency (a cache must initialise before a listener); destruction happens in reverse order.

expert.content:
Lifecycle management: Lifecycle and SmartLifecycle

• Lifecycle (start(), stop(), isRunning()) models beans with start/stop semantics (message listeners, schedulers, embedded servers). context.start()/stop() propagate to all Lifecycle beans. SmartLifecycle is started automatically at the end of refresh in phase order (lowest first at startup; highest first at shutdown), supports isAutoStartup() and an asynchronous stop with a callback: ideal for graceful shutdown (stop accepting work, drain queues).
• Graceful shutdown: Boot registers a JVM shutdown hook; the web server stops accepting requests (server.shutdown=graceful), in-flight work finishes within spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase, then beans are destroyed.

interviewQA: How does a child context find beans?
It looks in itself first and then in its parent contexts; parents cannot see child beans. This is how Spring MVC separates root (services) and servlet (controllers) contexts.
What is SmartLifecycle used for?
Beans that should start automatically after the context is ready and stop in a defined phase order with optional async stop, e.g. message listeners or schedulers needing graceful shutdown.
What does @DependsOn do?
It forces other named beans to be created first (and destroyed last) even when there is no direct dependency between the classes.

topics.name: The Complete Bean Lifecycle Order

beginner.content:
From definition to destruction

#PhaseMechanism
1Bean definition loadedScanning, @Bean, XML
2BeanFactoryPostProcessor modifies definitionsPlaceholders, overrides
3InstantiationConstructor / factory method
4Populate properties (dependency injection)Autowiring, @Value, setters
5BeanNameAware, BeanFactoryAware, ApplicationContextAware ...Aware callbacks
6BeanPostProcessor.postProcessBeforeInitializationIncludes @PostConstruct (via a BPP)
7@PostConstructJakarta annotation
8InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()Spring interface
9Custom init-method@Bean(initMethod)
10BeanPostProcessor.postProcessAfterInitializationAOP proxies created here
11Bean ready for useSingletons live until close
12@PreDestroyOn context close
13DisposableBean.destroy()Spring interface
14Custom destroy-methodInferred close()/shutdown() for @Bean

intermediate.content:
Notes on the lifecycle

• Steps 6 and 10 run for every bean: that is the extension point of the container. Steps 12-14 run only for singleton and custom-scoped beans when the context closes; prototype beans are handed to the caller and forgotten.
• If InitializingBean's afterPropertiesSet and a custom init method name the same method, it runs once. Constructor exceptions or init failures abort startup with BeanCreationException showing the chain of beans being created.
• Lazy singletons follow the same steps on first use; scoped beans per scope instance.

expert.content:
Lifecycle in practice: what to put where

• Constructor: assign injected fields only (no I/O, no calls to injected beans that may be proxies not yet ready). @PostConstruct: validate configuration, open resources, pre-compute lookup tables. BeanPostProcessor: framework-style cross-cutting logic for all beans. SmartLifecycle: start background work after the context is ready. ApplicationReadyEvent: tasks needing a fully started application. @PreDestroy: release resources quickly (the JVM may be about to exit; use a timeout).

interviewQA: Explain the Spring bean lifecycle.

Definitions are loaded and post-processed, the bean is instantiated, dependencies are injected, Aware callbacks run, BeanPostProcessor before-init, @PostConstruct, afterPropertiesSet, custom init, BeanPostProcessor after-init (proxies), the bean is used, then on close @PreDestroy, destroy() and custom destroy methods.
At which step are AOP proxies created?
In postProcessAfterInitialization by an auto-proxy creator BeanPostProcessor, so the object in the container (and injected elsewhere) is the proxy.
Which beans get destroy callbacks?
Singletons and custom-scoped beans managed by the container; prototype beans do not.

topics.name: BeanPostProcessor, BeanFactoryPostProcessor and BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor

beginner.content:
BeanPostProcessor (BPP)

• BeanPostProcessor intercepts bean instances around initialisation: postProcessBeforeInitialization and postProcessAfterInitialization (may return a replacement/wrapper). Built-ins: AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor (@Autowired/@Value), CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor (@PostConstruct/@Resource), ApplicationContextAwareProcessor, AnnotationAwareAspectJAutoProxyCreator (AOP), ScheduledAnnotationBeanPostProcessor (@Scheduled), AsyncAnnotationBeanPostProcessor.
• Sub-interfaces: InstantiationAwareBeanPostProcessor (before instantiation/property population), SmartInstantiationAwareBeanPostProcessor (early references, predict type), MergedBeanDefinitionPostProcessor, DestructionAwareBeanPostProcessor. Order with PriorityOrdered/Ordered.
• Declare BPP @Bean methods as static so the configuration class is not instantiated early; BPPs and the beans they depend on are created before regular beans so are not post-processed themselves ("not eligible for auto-proxying").

intermediate.content:
BeanFactoryPostProcessor (BFPP)

• BeanFactoryPostProcessor.postProcessBeanFactory(ConfigurableListableBeanFactory) works on bean definitions (metadata) before any bean is instantiated: change property values, scope, lazy flag, register aliases. Built-ins: PropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurer (resolves ${...}), PropertyOverrideConfigurer, CustomScopeConfigurer, CustomEditorConfigurer, EventListenerMethodProcessor.
• BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor (extends BFPP) runs first and can add or remove bean definitions: ConfigurationClassPostProcessor is one: it parses @Configuration, @ComponentScan, @Import and registers every @Bean.
• Do not obtain beans in a BFPP (it forces early instantiation, skipping other post-processors).

expert.content:
BPP vs BFPP

BeanFactoryPostProcessorBeanPostProcessor
Operates onBean definitions (metadata)Bean instances
WhenBefore any regular bean is instantiatedFor each bean around initialisation
Typical usePlaceholders, register definitions, change scopeAnnotation processing, proxies, validation
ExamplesConfigurationClassPostProcessor, PropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurerAutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor, auto-proxy creator
Return valuevoidThe (possibly replaced) bean

interviewQA: BeanPostProcessor vs BeanFactoryPostProcessor?

BFPP modifies bean definitions before beans exist (e.g. resolves placeholders, registers definitions); BPP intercepts bean instances before/after initialisation and can wrap them (e.g. autowiring, AOP proxies).
Why make BeanPostProcessor @Bean methods static?
Post-processors are created very early; a non-static method would force the enclosing configuration class to be instantiated too early, so it and its beans miss other post-processing.
How do @Autowired and @PostConstruct work?
AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor and CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor are BPPs that inject dependencies and invoke @PostConstruct methods during bean creation.

topics.name: Lifecycle Callbacks, Lifecycle Events, Ordering and Debugging Lifecycle Issues

beginner.content:
Context lifecycle events and graceful stop

• The context publishes: ContextRefreshedEvent (all singletons ready), ContextStartedEvent/ContextStoppedEvent (start()/stop()), ContextClosedEvent (closing). Boot adds ApplicationStartingEvent, ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEvent, ApplicationPreparedEvent, ApplicationStartedEvent, ApplicationReadyEvent (ready for requests), AvailabilityChangeEvent (liveness/readiness), ApplicationFailedEvent.
• Use ApplicationReadyEvent or an ApplicationRunner for startup work that needs the full app (data loading, warming, registering with service discovery), not @PostConstruct.

intermediate.content:
Ordering of beans and callbacks

• Creation order follows dependencies; unrelated singletons are created in definition registration order (scanning order is not guaranteed: do not rely on it; use @DependsOn). Ordering of collections (List<X>) and of post-processors/listeners/aspects uses @Order, Ordered, @Priority (lower value = higher priority; PriorityOrdered beats Ordered). @Order on a bean does not control instantiation order, only position in injected lists and execution order of ordered contracts.

expert.content:
Debugging lifecycle issues

• Symptoms and causes: (1) @Autowired field is null → the object was created with new or the class is not a bean / not scanned; (2) @Transactional or @Async ignored → self-invocation, non-public method, final class/method, bean created too early by a BPP/BFPP ("not eligible for getting processed by all BeanPostProcessors"); (3) @PostConstruct not called → missing jakarta.annotation processing (not an ApplicationContext) or wrong signature; (4) @PreDestroy not called on a prototype or killed JVM; (5) UnsatisfiedDependencyException with long chain → read the root cause at the bottom.
• Tools: logging.level.org.springframework.beans.factory=DEBUG, Actuator /actuator/beans, /actuator/conditions, /actuator/startup, IDE breakpoints in AbstractAutowireCapableBeanFactory.doCreateBean, AopUtils.isAopProxy(bean) and bean.getClass() to see whether you hold a proxy.

interviewQA: Which events does the application context publish?
ContextRefreshedEvent, ContextStartedEvent, ContextStoppedEvent and ContextClosedEvent; Spring Boot adds Application Starting/EnvironmentPrepared/Prepared/Started/Ready/Failed events.
Does @Order control the order beans are created?
No. It orders items within injected collections and ordered contracts (aspects, filters, listeners); creation order follows dependencies and @DependsOn.
Why is my @PostConstruct or @Transactional not working?
Usually the object is not a container-managed bean (created with new), is invoked through self-invocation bypassing the proxy, or the bean was created before the relevant post-processor existed.

topics.name: SpEL Basics: Expressions, Literals, Properties, Methods, Operators

beginner.content:
What is SpEL?

• SpEL is a powerful expression language that can query and manipulate an object graph at runtime, used in @Value("#{...}"), XML, @ConditionalOnExpression, @Cacheable(condition=...), @PreAuthorize, Spring Data @Query, Spring Integration. The API: ExpressionParser (SpelExpressionParser), Expression, EvaluationContext (StandardEvaluationContext or the safer SimpleEvaluationContext). Expressions are written #{...} in annotations (placeholders use ${...}).

intermediate.content:
Property and method access, operators

• Property navigation uses getters: user.address.city; safe navigation user?.address?.city avoids NPE; collection selection list.?[age > 18] (filter), list.^[...] first, list.$[...] last; projection list.![name] maps. Operators: arithmetic (+ - * / % ^), relational (== != < > <= >= between instanceof matches or textual eq ne lt gt le ge), logical (and or not), ternary cond ? a : b, Elvis name ?: 'default', assignment, regex matches, inline lists {1,2,3} and maps {name:'A', age:3}, array construction, type operator T(), constructor new ...(), variables #var, #this, #root, bean reference @beanName.

expert.content:
Variables, functions and context

• EvaluationContext.setVariable("name", value) → #name; registerFunction("fn", Method) → #fn(...); setRootObject; BeanResolver enables @beanName references (done in the container). Use SimpleEvaluationContext (read-only data binding, no type references or constructors) when evaluating untrusted expressions: a full StandardEvaluationContext can call arbitrary methods (T(Runtime).getRuntime().exec(...)), a remote-code-execution risk (SpEL injection).
• Expressions can be compiled for speed (SpelCompilerMode.IMMEDIATE).

interviewQA: What is SpEL used for?
Runtime expression evaluation on object graphs: @Value("#{...}"), conditions in @Cacheable/@Conditional/@PreAuthorize, XML configuration and Spring Data queries.
Difference between ${...} and #{...}?
${...} is a property placeholder resolved from the Environment; #{...} is a SpEL expression evaluated against beans and objects; they can be combined: #{'${list}'.split(',')}.
Why is SpEL a security concern?

With StandardEvaluationContext an expression can invoke arbitrary types and methods, so evaluating user input leads to remote code execution; use SimpleEvaluationContext or avoid evaluating untrusted input.

topics.name: SpEL in @Value, Bean References, Conditions and Practical Usage

beginner.content:
SpEL in annotations and configuration

• In @Value you can reference other beans (#{courseService.defaultLevel}), system properties/environment (#{systemProperties['user.home']}, #{systemEnvironment['HOME']}), call static methods (#{T(java.lang.Math).random() * 100}), compute values and select collections. Combine with placeholders: #{'${app.tags}'.split(',')} or #{${app.base} * 2}.

intermediate.content:
SpEL in conditions, caching, security and queries

• @ConditionalOnExpression("${feature.x:false} and '${env}' == 'prod'"); @Cacheable(key = "#course.id", condition = "#course.published", unless = "#result == null"); @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN') or #userId == authentication.principal.id"); @EventListener(condition = "#event.amount > 1000"); @Scheduled(cron = "#{@config.cron}"); Spring Data JPA @Query("select c from Course c where c.owner = ?#{principal.username}").
• Method-argument names are exposed as #name (compile with -parameters) or #p0/#a0; the result as #result and the root #root.methodName/#root.target.

expert.content:
Best practices and limitations

• Keep expressions short and declarative; they are strings, so errors appear only at runtime and refactoring tools do not track them. Move logic into a bean method and call it (#{@pricing.discount(#root)} or a real method). Prefer @ConfigurationProperties over many @Value SpEL expressions for structured configuration. Cache parsed Expression objects (they are thread-safe) if evaluating repeatedly. In native images SpEL needs reflection hints.

interviewQA: How can SpEL reference another bean?
Inside Spring-managed expressions with #{beanName.property} or @beanName in contexts with a BeanResolver (e.g. #{@pricing.rate()}).
How do you use SpEL in @Cacheable?
With key, condition and unless attributes, referencing method arguments (#id), the result (#result) and root metadata, e.g. key="#course.id", unless="#result == null".
When should you avoid SpEL?
For complex logic or untrusted input; use plain Java methods and @ConfigurationProperties for maintainability and safety.

topics.name: Application Events: Publishing and Listening

beginner.content:
The event model

• Spring's event mechanism is an in-process publish/subscribe (Observer pattern) built on ApplicationEventPublisher and ApplicationEventMulticaster. Publishers do not know listeners: loose coupling between modules (order → notification, audit, search indexing). Events can be any object since Spring 4.2 (no need to extend ApplicationEvent); using records is idiomatic.
• Publish: inject ApplicationEventPublisher and call publishEvent(event). Listen: @EventListener method (parameter type selects the event; supports polymorphism and generics) or ApplicationListener<E>. By default delivery is synchronous in the publisher's thread and transaction: a listener exception propagates to the publisher.

intermediate.content:
Listener features

• Filtering with SpEL condition; ordering with @Order; generics: @EventListener on EntityCreated<Course> works with ResolvableTypeProvider; return value publishes a follow-up event (a returned object or collection is published); listening to several event types with @EventListener({A.class, B.class}) (no parameter or a common supertype); SmartApplicationListener for programmatic filtering.

expert.content:
Built-in events and the ApplicationEvent class

• Framework events: ContextRefreshedEvent, ContextStartedEvent, ContextStoppedEvent, ContextClosedEvent, RequestHandledEvent (web), Boot's ApplicationReadyEvent etc. Extending ApplicationEvent (with source, timestamp) is optional; use it when you want a source object or legacy compatibility.
• Class-based style: class OrderPlaced extends ApplicationEvent + implements ApplicationListener<OrderPlaced>: verbose, but explicit.

interviewQA: How do Spring events work?

A publisher calls ApplicationEventPublisher.publishEvent; the multicaster delivers the event to all matching listeners (@EventListener or ApplicationListener), synchronously in the caller's thread by default.
Does the event have to extend ApplicationEvent?
No. Since Spring 4.2 any object can be an event; it is wrapped in a PayloadApplicationEvent internally.
What happens if a listener throws an exception?
With synchronous delivery the exception propagates to the publisher and can roll back its transaction; async listeners need their own error handling.

topics.name: Async Events, Transactional Events, Custom Multicaster and Best Practices

beginner.content:
Asynchronous events

• Add @Async to a listener (with @EnableAsync) to run it on a TaskExecutor; or configure the multicaster with an executor to make all listeners async. Trade-offs: the publisher no longer waits, exceptions are not propagated (use AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler), the listener runs outside the publisher's transaction and security context, and ordering is lost. Use a bounded ThreadPoolTaskExecutor (or virtual threads) so a burst of events cannot exhaust resources.

intermediate.content:
Transactional events (@TransactionalEventListener)

• Problem: a normal listener runs inside the publisher's transaction, so it can send an email for data that then rolls back, or read rows not yet committed from another thread. @TransactionalEventListener(phase = ...) binds delivery to a transaction phase: AFTER_COMMIT (default: only if it committed), AFTER_ROLLBACK, AFTER_COMPLETION, BEFORE_COMMIT. If no transaction is active the event is dropped unless fallbackExecution = true.
• In AFTER_COMMIT the transaction is already over; if the listener needs to write to the database use @Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW). For guaranteed delivery across crashes use the transactional outbox pattern or Spring Modulith's event publication registry instead of in-memory events.

expert.content:
Custom events and multicaster, best practices

• A custom ApplicationEventMulticaster bean (name applicationEventMulticaster) can add error handling (setErrorHandler), async execution or filtering. Best practices: events are facts in the past tense (CourseEnrolled), immutable and small (ids, not entities); use them to decouple modules, not as a general method-call replacement; avoid deep event chains (hard to debug); remember events are in-process only (use a broker for cross-service); do not rely on listener order; make listeners idempotent; test with @RecordApplicationEvents.

interviewQA: How do you make an event listener asynchronous?
Annotate the listener with @Async (and @EnableAsync) or give the application event multicaster a TaskExecutor; exceptions then do not reach the publisher and the transaction is not shared.
What is @TransactionalEventListener?
A listener bound to a transaction phase (AFTER_COMMIT by default, also BEFORE_COMMIT, AFTER_ROLLBACK, AFTER_COMPLETION) so side effects such as emails happen only after the data is committed.
Are Spring events suitable for communication between microservices?
No. They are in-process; use a message broker (Kafka, RabbitMQ) with an outbox for reliable cross-service events.

topics.name: AOP Concepts: Cross-Cutting Concerns, Aspect, Join Point, Pointcut, Advice, Weaving

beginner.content:
Why AOP?

• Cross-cutting concerns (logging, transactions, security, caching, metrics, retries, auditing) cut across many classes. Without AOP the code is scattered (same lines everywhere) and tangled (business logic mixed with infrastructure). AOP modularises them into aspects applied declaratively. Spring's own @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async, @Retryable, @PreAuthorize are all AOP.
• OOP vs AOP: OOP modularises by class (vertical); AOP modularises concerns that cross classes (horizontal).

intermediate.content:
AOP terminology

TermMeaningExample
AspectA module that encapsulates a cross-cutting concern (pointcuts + advice)@Aspect class LoggingAspect
Join pointA point in program execution where advice can apply; in Spring AOP always a method executionCalling OrderService.place()
PointcutA predicate selecting join pointsexecution(* com.jsl.service.*.*(..))
AdviceCode to run at a join point (before, after, around ...)@Before, @Around
Target objectThe bean being advisedOrderService
ProxyThe object created by AOP wrapping the targetJDK/CGLIB proxy
WeavingLinking aspects with targets: compile-time, load-time or runtime (Spring proxies)AspectJ vs Spring AOP
IntroductionAdding interfaces/members to a target@DeclareParents

expert.content:
Spring AOP vs AspectJ

Spring AOPAspectJ
WeavingRuntime, proxy-basedCompile-time, post-compile or load-time bytecode weaving
Join pointsPublic method execution on Spring beansMethods, constructors, field access, static init, any object
Self-invocationNot advised (call bypasses proxy)Advised
PerformanceSlight proxy overheadFaster (no proxy)
SetupEasy: @EnableAspectJAutoProxy (auto in Boot)Needs weaver/agent or compiler plugin
Use90% of enterprise needsAdvanced needs: advise non-bean objects, self-invocation, field access
• Spring AOP uses AspectJ's annotations and pointcut language but not its weaver (unless you enable it with @EnableLoadTimeWeaving/mode=ASPECTJ for @Transactional).
codeExamples:
<!-- Boot: spring-boot-starter-aop -->
<dependency><groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId><artifactId>spring-boot-starter-aop</artifactId></dependency>

@Configuration @EnableAspectJAutoProxy          // plain Spring (Boot auto-configures it)
class AopConfig {}

interviewQA: What is AOP?
A programming approach that modularises cross-cutting concerns such as logging, security and transactions into aspects applied to methods declaratively, so business code stays clean.
Spring AOP vs AspectJ?

Spring AOP is runtime proxy-based and only advises public method executions of Spring beans; AspectJ weaves bytecode at compile/load time and supports all join points including constructors, fields and self-invocation.
What is a join point in Spring AOP?
Always a method execution on a Spring-managed bean (proxy-based AOP does not support field or constructor join points).

topics.name: Writing Aspects: Advice Types, Pointcut Expressions, JoinPoint and Ordering

beginner.content:
Advice types

AdviceRunsCan change result?
@BeforeBefore the method; cannot stop it (except by throwing)No
@AfterReturningAfter normal return; access returning valueInspect only
@AfterThrowingAfter an exception; access throwingNo (rethrown)
@After (finally)Always, after return or exceptionNo
@AroundWraps the call; you decide whether to call proceed(), with what args, and what to returnYes
• Order for one aspect around a normal call: @Around (before proceed) → @Before → method → @AfterReturning/@AfterThrowing → @After → @Around (after proceed). Prefer the least powerful advice that does the job (@Around is easy to misuse: forgetting proceed() skips the method, swallowing exceptions hides failures).

intermediate.content:
Pointcut expressions

• Designators: execution(modifiers? return declaring-type? name(params) throws?) (the main one), within(type pattern), this (proxy type) / target (target type), args(...) (argument types, binds arguments), @annotation(Ann) (method has annotation; binds it), @within(Ann) (class has annotation), @target, @args, bean(name*) (Spring-specific). Combine with &&, ||, !.
• Wildcards: * any single element, .. any subpackages or any parameters, + subtypes.

expert.content:
JoinPoint API, argument binding, ordering and a real aspect

• JoinPoint: getSignature() (MethodSignature → method, return type, parameter names), getArgs(), getTarget(), getThis() (the proxy), toShortString(). ProceedingJoinPoint adds proceed() and proceed(Object[] newArgs). Ordering of aspects: @Order(n) (lower = outermost/runs first before, last after) or Ordered; unordered aspects have no defined order. Put security before transaction before logging intentionally.

interviewQA: Explain the types of advice.
@Before, @AfterReturning, @AfterThrowing, @After (finally) and @Around; around advice wraps the call, controls proceed(), arguments and return value, and is the most powerful but easiest to misuse.
Difference between execution and within pointcuts?
execution matches method signatures (return type, name, params); within matches all join points inside types in a package or class.
How do you order multiple aspects?
Use @Order or implement Ordered: lower values have higher precedence, running first on the way in and last on the way out.

topics.name: Real-World AOP: Transactions, Logging, Caching, Security, Exception Handling and Pitfalls

beginner.content:
AOP in practice

• Declarative transactions (TransactionInterceptor via @Transactional), caching (CacheInterceptor), security (MethodSecurityInterceptor/@PreAuthorize), async (AnnotationAsyncExecutionInterceptor), validation (@Validated method validation), metrics (@Timed/@Observed), retry (Spring Retry), audit, request logging with correlation id, exception translation (repositories). For your own: logging, auditing, rate limiting, feature flags, tenant routing.

intermediate.content:
Common AOP pitfalls

• Self-invocation: this.method() inside the same class bypasses the proxy, so the advice (and @Transactional/@Async/@Cacheable) is skipped. Fix: move the method to another bean, inject the proxy of yourself (@Lazy self), use AopContext.currentProxy() (exposeProxy=true), or AspectJ mode.
• Only public methods (CGLIB can advise protected/package-private in some cases since 6.0, but do not rely on it); final classes/methods cannot be CGLIB-proxied; private methods never advised; non-bean objects (new) never advised; constructors/fields not supported.
• Proxy type surprises: injecting the concrete class when the bean is a JDK proxy fails (BeanNotOfRequiredTypeException); Boot defaults to CGLIB (spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true). Performance: broad pointcuts (execution(* *(..))) slow startup and calls. Swallowing exceptions in @Around changes behaviour and breaks rollbacks. Aspect order matters (retry outside transaction, not inside).

expert.content:
Testing aspects and the AOP checklist

• Test an aspect with a small AspectJProxyFactory (unit) or @SpringBootTest(classes = {AuditAspect.class, Target.class}) with @EnableAspectJAutoProxy (integration). Checklist: narrow pointcuts; named pointcuts for reuse; @Around only when needed; always rethrow exceptions; never do slow work in advice on hot paths; keep aspects stateless; document order; verify the bean is a proxy (AopUtils).

interviewQA: Why does @Transactional not work on a method called from within the same class?
Self-invocation calls the target directly, not the proxy, so the interceptor never runs; call through another bean or the proxy.
What cannot Spring AOP advise?
Private/final methods, final classes (CGLIB), objects not managed by Spring, constructors and field access; use AspectJ for those.
Name real Spring features built on AOP.
@Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async, @PreAuthorize/@Secured, @Validated method validation, @Retryable, @Observed metrics and repository exception translation.

topics.name: Proxy Pattern, JDK Dynamic Proxy vs CGLIB Proxy, and How Spring Chooses

beginner.content:
The proxy pattern in Spring

• A proxy is a stand-in object with the same type as the target that intercepts calls, adds behaviour (transaction, security, cache, async, lazy loading) and delegates to the real target. Spring creates proxies during bean post-processing (postProcessAfterInitialization of AbstractAutoProxyCreator) and puts the proxy in the container, so every injection point receives the proxy.
• Two mechanisms: JDK dynamic proxy (java.lang.reflect.Proxy, implements the target's interfaces) and CGLIB (generates a subclass of the target class at runtime; Spring repackages it as org.springframework.cglib and since Spring 4 uses Objenesis so no default constructor is needed).

intermediate.content:
JDK proxy vs CGLIB proxy

JDK dynamic proxyCGLIB proxy
RequiresThe target implements at least one interfaceA non-final class (works without interfaces)
Mechanismjava.lang.reflect.Proxy implementing interfacesGenerated subclass overriding methods
Proxy typeOnly the interface types (cannot inject the concrete class)Subclass of target: injectable by class or interface
LimitationsOnly interface methods are advisedFinal classes/methods and private methods cannot be overridden
ConstructorNot involvedTarget constructor not called for proxy (Objenesis); target is a separate instance
PerformanceReflection; fine in modern JVMsSimilar; faster dispatch historically
Spring Boot defaultCGLIB for AOP and @Transactional (spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true)
• Decision in Spring: if proxyTargetClass=false (plain Spring default) and the target implements an interface → JDK proxy; otherwise CGLIB. Boot, and @EnableAspectJAutoProxy(proxyTargetClass = true), force CGLIB. Configuration classes are always CGLIB-enhanced.

expert.content:
Proxy utilities and how to see what you have

• AopUtils.isAopProxy(o), isJdkDynamicProxy, isCglibProxy, AopUtils.getTargetClass(o), AopProxyUtils.ultimateTargetClass, ((Advised) proxy).getTargetSource().getTarget(). ProxyFactory builds proxies programmatically (addAdvice, setProxyTargetClass, setTarget). ProxyFactoryBean is the XML-era equivalent. In a CGLIB proxy the class name shows $$SpringCGLIB$$.

interviewQA: JDK dynamic proxy vs CGLIB?

JDK proxies implement the target's interfaces via java.lang.reflect.Proxy; CGLIB generates a subclass of the target class so it works without interfaces but cannot override final classes or methods. Spring Boot uses CGLIB by default.
Why does injecting the concrete class fail with a JDK proxy?

The proxy implements only the interfaces and is not an instance of the implementation class, so injection by the class type fails with BeanNotOfRequiredTypeException; inject the interface or use CGLIB.
How does Spring decide the proxy type?
JDK proxy when the target implements an interface and proxyTargetClass is false; otherwise CGLIB; Boot sets proxyTargetClass=true by default.

topics.name: Proxy Limitations, Self-Invocation, Final Methods, Proxy Chaining and Debugging

beginner.content:
Why self-invocation bypasses the proxy

• The proxy wraps the target: client → proxy → interceptors → target.method(). Inside the target, this is the raw target, so this.other() calls the other method directly; no interceptor runs. This is the cause of "@Transactional / @Async / @Cacheable does nothing" bugs.
• Solutions ranked: (1) restructure: move the advised method to another bean; (2) inject the proxy of yourself (@Autowired @Lazy MyService self); (3) AopContext.currentProxy() with @EnableAspectJAutoProxy(exposeProxy = true); (4) AspectJ weaving (mode = AdviceMode.ASPECTJ); (5) TransactionTemplate for programmatic control.

intermediate.content:
Other proxy limitations

• final class → CGLIB cannot subclass (Spring fails at startup or skips). final/private/static methods → not intercepted (CGLIB can't override). Package-private/protected: supported by CGLIB when the proxy is in the same package/classloader; @Transactional on non-public methods works only for class-based proxies from Spring 6.0 but is bad practice. Field access on a CGLIB proxy reads the proxy's (uninitialised) fields, not the target's: always use getters. equals/hashCode/toString behave on the proxy; compare via the target if needed. Constructor side effects are not repeated for the proxy. Kotlin classes are final by default: use the kotlin-spring (all-open) plugin.
• Serialization of proxies and reflection that inspects getClass() / annotations on the proxy class: use AopUtils.getTargetClass or AnnotationUtils.findAnnotation.

expert.content:
Proxy chaining, ordering and debugging

• A bean can be wrapped by several advisors in one proxy (Spring builds a single proxy with an advisor chain: transaction, security, cache, custom aspect, ordered by @Order / Ordered); it does not stack proxies. Typical practical order: Retry → Security → Transaction → Cache → target (retry must be outside the transaction; @EnableTransactionManagement(order=...), @EnableCaching(order=...), @EnableRetry(order=...)).
• Debug: logging.level.org.springframework.aop=DEBUG, Advised.getAdvisors(), set a breakpoint in CglibAopProxy.DynamicAdvisedInterceptor.intercept / JdkDynamicAopProxy.invoke, look at the stack trace: it shows ReflectiveMethodInvocation.proceed frames for each interceptor, and use -Dcglib.debugLocation to dump generated classes.

interviewQA: Why does this.method() not trigger advice?
Inside the target the reference is the raw object, not the proxy, so the call skips the interceptor chain; call through another bean, an injected self reference or AopContext.currentProxy().
What happens when you put @Transactional on a final method?
CGLIB cannot override it, so the call is not intercepted and runs without a transaction (no error), a common silent bug; avoid final on proxied classes.
Does Spring stack a proxy per aspect?
No: one proxy per bean with a chain of advisors ordered by precedence.

topics.name: Scoped Proxies, Lazy Resolution Proxies, Transaction/Security Proxies and Proxies vs Native Images

beginner.content:
Other proxies the container creates

• Scoped proxy (ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS/INTERFACES): a singleton proxy that looks up the target from the current scope on every call (request/session beans). Lazy-resolution proxy (@Lazy injection point): resolves the real bean on first use. Configuration class proxy (CGLIB subclass for @Bean method interception). Repository proxies (Spring Data creates a JDK proxy implementing your interface backed by SimpleJpaRepository). Feign/HTTP interface proxies. Transaction proxy (TransactionInterceptor) and security proxy (AuthorizationManagerBeforeMethodInterceptor) are advisors in the AOP proxy.

intermediate.content:
Proxies and Ahead-of-Time (native image) processing

• GraalVM native images cannot generate classes at runtime. Spring 6's AOT engine pre-computes bean definitions and registers runtime hints; CGLIB proxies for @Configuration are generated at build time, JDK proxy interface sets must be declared (RuntimeHints.proxies().registerJdkProxy(...)). Dynamic behaviour such as conditions on property values at runtime, @Profile changes, ImportSelector logic must be fixed at build time.
• Practical advice: prefer interfaces and constructor injection, avoid reflection-heavy tricks, provide RuntimeHintsRegistrar for custom proxies/resources.

expert.content:
Choosing a proxy strategy

• Prefer constructor injection of interfaces and let Boot use CGLIB; keep proxied classes non-final with public methods; do not store state in fields of proxied beans that other beans read directly; use ObjectProvider instead of scoped proxies when you want the lookup to be explicit; check with AopUtils if something is not intercepted; and remember proxies add a small cost per call, so keep very hot inner-loop methods outside advised beans.

interviewQA: What is a scoped proxy?
A singleton stand-in injected into longer-lived beans that resolves the actual target (request/session scoped instance) on every call.
How do proxies affect GraalVM native images?
Classes cannot be generated at runtime, so Spring AOT pre-generates CGLIB proxies and you must register JDK proxy interfaces and reflection via runtime hints.
How does Spring Data create a repository implementation?
At startup it creates a JDK dynamic proxy implementing your repository interface that delegates to a generic implementation (e.g. SimpleJpaRepository) and query interceptors.

topics.name: Resource Abstraction: Resource, ResourceLoader, ResourcePatternResolver and Resource Injection

beginner.content:
The Resource abstraction

• org.springframework.core.io.Resource abstracts access to files, classpath entries, URLs, servlet context paths, byte arrays and input streams: exists(), isReadable(), getInputStream(), getFile(), getURL(), contentLength(). Implementations: ClassPathResource, FileSystemResource, UrlResource, ServletContextResource, ByteArrayResource, InputStreamResource, PathResource.
• Location prefixes: classpath:, classpath*: (all matching entries on the classpath, including jars), file:, http:/https:; no prefix → depends on the context.

intermediate.content:
ResourceLoader and ResourcePatternResolver

• ResourceLoader.getResource("classpath:..."): every ApplicationContext is a ResourceLoader. ResourcePatternResolver.getResources("classpath*:/config/*.xml") supports Ant-style wildcards (*, **, ?). PathMatchingResourcePatternResolver is the standard implementation. Inject resources directly with @Value("classpath:data/courses.json") Resource courses or @Value("classpath*:schemas/*.json") Resource[] schemas.
• ResourceLoaderAware or constructor-injected ResourceLoader to load dynamically. Spring Boot's spring.config.location uses the same mechanism.

expert.content:
Resource best practices

• Never assume a resource is a file (it is inside a jar in production); use streams. Close streams (try-with-resources). Use classpath*: to gather resources from multiple jars. Use Resource parameters in your APIs instead of String paths so callers can pass any source. Security: never build resource locations from user input (path traversal: ../../etc/passwd); validate and normalise (StringUtils.cleanPath, Path.normalize() and a base-directory check).

interviewQA: What is the Spring Resource abstraction?
A uniform interface to read resources from classpath, files, URLs or streams, with ResourceLoader resolving location strings by prefix and ResourcePatternResolver supporting wildcards.
classpath: vs classpath*:?
classpath: returns the first match on the classpath; classpath*: returns all matching resources from every classpath root (all jars).
Why use getInputStream() rather than getFile()?
Resources inside a packaged jar are not files on disk, so getFile() fails; streams work everywhere.

topics.name: i18n with MessageSource, Type Conversion, Formatting and Data Binding

beginner.content:
MessageSource (internationalisation)

• MessageSource resolves messages by code and Locale: getMessage(code, args, defaultMessage, locale). ResourceBundleMessageSource / ReloadableResourceBundleMessageSource read messages.properties, messages_hi.properties ... with {0} placeholders (MessageFormat). Boot configures it from spring.messages.basename=messages. The ApplicationContext is itself a MessageSource (bean named messageSource). In MVC the LocaleResolver (Accept-Language, cookie, session) picks the locale.

intermediate.content:
Type conversion and formatting

• ConversionService (core.convert): the modern, thread-safe type conversion SPI: Converter<S,T>, ConverterFactory, GenericConverter; register in DefaultConversionService/FormattingConversionService (WebMvcConfigurer.addFormatters). Used for @Value, request parameters, @ConfigurationProperties ("5s" → Duration, "10MB" → DataSize). Formatter<T> (format/parse with locale) and @DateTimeFormat/@NumberFormat. Legacy PropertyEditor (CustomEditorConfigurer) is stateful and not thread-safe: avoid in new code.

expert.content:
Data binding

• DataBinder binds property values (a Map/request params) onto an object using BeanWrapper (nested paths address.city, indexed items[0].name), converts types and collects BindingResult errors; used by MVC form binding, @ModelAttribute and Boot's Binder for @ConfigurationProperties. Protect against mass assignment: restrict bindable fields (setAllowedFields, DTOs).

interviewQA: How does Spring support internationalisation?
Through MessageSource (resource bundles with locale-specific property files) plus a LocaleResolver in web apps; messages are resolved by code with arguments for the current Locale.
Converter vs Formatter vs PropertyEditor?
Converter is a general, thread-safe S→T conversion; Formatter adds locale-aware parse/print for text; PropertyEditor is the older stateful, non-thread-safe mechanism that should be avoided.
What is mass assignment and how does binding mitigate it?
Attackers set fields you did not intend to expose; restrict bindable fields with DataBinder allowed fields or bind to dedicated DTOs.

topics.name: Spring Utilities, Task Execution and Scheduling, and Caching Abstraction

beginner.content:
Everyday utility classes

• Assert (notNull, hasText, isTrue with messages), StringUtils (hasText, cleanPath, commaDelimitedListToSet), CollectionUtils, ObjectUtils, ClassUtils, ReflectionUtils, BeanUtils (copyProperties, instantiateClass), AnnotationUtils/AnnotatedElementUtils, StopWatch, FileCopyUtils/StreamUtils, UriComponentsBuilder, HtmlUtils.htmlEscape, Base64Utils (use java.util.Base64), DigestUtils, PropertiesLoaderUtils. They are static helpers: prefer JDK equivalents when they exist.

intermediate.content:
Task execution and scheduling

• TaskExecutor (ThreadPoolTaskExecutor, SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor with virtual threads: spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true), @EnableAsync + @Async (return void/CompletableFuture; needs the proxy: self-invocation caveat; define your own executor, the default unbounded SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor is risky), @EnableScheduling + @Scheduled (fixedRate, fixedDelay, initialDelay, cron with zone). Default scheduler has one thread: long jobs delay others: configure a TaskScheduler pool. In clusters every instance runs the job: use ShedLock or Quartz.

expert.content:
Caching abstraction

• @EnableCaching adds proxy-based caching: @Cacheable (look up; run method on miss and store), @CachePut (always run and update), @CacheEvict (remove; allEntries, beforeInvocation), @Caching, @CacheConfig. Keys by SpEL (key), condition, unless. Providers via CacheManager: ConcurrentMapCacheManager (dev), Caffeine (local, TTL/size), Redis (distributed), Ehcache, Hazelcast. Same proxy rules apply (public method, external call). Cache immutable, small objects; define TTL; beware stale data and cache stampede.

interviewQA: Why configure your own executor for @Async?
The default executor creates unbounded threads (SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor); a bounded ThreadPoolTaskExecutor (or virtual threads) protects the application and lets you set names and rejection policy.
What are the pitfalls of @Scheduled in a cluster?
Each instance runs the job; use a distributed lock (ShedLock) or Quartz clustering. The default scheduler has a single thread, so configure a pool for several jobs.
@Cacheable vs @CachePut?
@Cacheable skips the method when a cached value exists; @CachePut always runs the method and stores the result, used for updates.

topics.name: Profiles: @Profile, Activation, Groups, Expressions and Environment-Specific Beans

beginner.content:
Profiles

• A profile is a named set of beans/configuration active only in some environments. @Profile("dev") on a @Component/@Configuration/@Bean; expressions @Profile("!prod"), @Profile("dev | local"), @Profile("cloud & !k8s") (use parentheses to mix operators). Beans with no profile are always created. Default profile: default (active when none set; change with spring.profiles.default).
• Activation: spring.profiles.active=dev,metrics (property/env SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE/CLI --spring.profiles.active/JVM -D), SpringApplication.setAdditionalProfiles, environment.setActiveProfiles, @ActiveProfiles in tests, spring.profiles.include (Boot 2.4+: use profile groups).

intermediate.content:
Profile-specific properties and best practices

• Boot loads application.yml, then application-{profile}.yml (profile values override); multi-document YAML with spring.config.activate.on-profile. Tests: @ActiveProfiles("test"); also @Profile on @TestConfiguration.
• Best practices: profiles select environment/behaviour variants, not every property (use externalised config for values); avoid too many profiles and do not store secrets in profile files; keep prod-like behaviour in default and put dev conveniences in a local profile (safer if the profile is forgotten); never use a prod profile to enable safety checks.
• Check: Environment.getActiveProfiles(), environment.acceptsProfiles(Profiles.of("prod")), Actuator /actuator/env.
codeExamples:
# application.yml
spring.application.name: catalogue
server.port: 8080
---
spring:
  config.activate.on-profile: local
  datasource.url: jdbc:h2:mem:jsl
logging.level.com.javaschoollab: DEBUG
---
spring:
  config.activate.on-profile: prod
  datasource.url: ${DB_URL}
logging.level.root: WARN

@SpringBootTest @ActiveProfiles("test") class CatalogueIT { }

expert.content:
Testing and verifying profile configurations

• Test each profile combination you ship: a @SpringBootTest with @ActiveProfiles proves the context starts and the expected beans exist; ApplicationContextRunner verifies conditional configuration quickly. In CI also start the app with the production profile and fake infrastructure to catch missing properties early. Log the active profiles at startup so deployments are traceable.

interviewQA: How do profiles work?
Beans or configuration annotated with @Profile are registered only if the profile expression matches the active profiles set via spring.profiles.active, environment APIs or @ActiveProfiles in tests.
What is a profile group?
A Boot 2.4+ feature letting one profile name activate several others (spring.profiles.group.prod=db,mq,metrics).
Why avoid a prod-only safety configuration?
If someone forgets to activate the profile the application starts without safeguards; make the safe behaviour default and relax it in local/dev.

topics.name: Externalized Configuration: Property Sources, Precedence, @ConfigurationProperties and Type-Safe Binding

beginner.content:
Property sources and precedence (Spring Boot)

• Boot reads configuration from many sources into the Environment. Highest to lowest (simplified): command-line args (--server.port=9000) → SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON → JVM system properties (-D) → OS environment variables (SERVER_PORT, relaxed binding) → application-{profile} files outside the jar → files inside the jar → application.yml/.properties → @PropertySource → defaults. Also spring.config.import (config server, configtree:/run/secrets/, Vault). Relaxed binding: my.main-color, my.mainColor, MY_MAINCOLOR all bind to mainColor.
• 12-factor: config in the environment; one artifact, many environments; secrets from the platform (Kubernetes Secrets, Vault), never in git.
codeExamples:
# precedence demo: later sources override earlier ones
# application.yml                  app.timeout: 5s
# application-prod.yml             app.timeout: 10s
# env var                          APP_TIMEOUT=15s
# java -jar app.jar --app.timeout=30s     <- wins

# import more config
spring.config.import: optional:file:./local.yml, optional:configserver:http://config:8888, configtree:/run/secrets/

@Value("${app.timeout}") Duration timeout;          // 30s

intermediate.content:
@ConfigurationProperties

• @ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.mail") binds a whole property subtree to a typed object (records and constructor binding in Boot 3: no @ConstructorBinding needed for a single constructor), with nested objects, lists, maps, Duration/DataSize conversion, @DefaultValue and validation (@Validated + Jakarta constraints) so bad config fails at startup. Enable with @EnableConfigurationProperties(X.class) or @ConfigurationPropertiesScan. Benefits over @Value: structure, validation, IDE metadata (spring-boot-configuration-processor), relaxed binding, refactor-friendly.

expert.content:
Property sources in plain Spring and refreshing configuration

• Plain Spring: @PropertySource, PropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurer, Environment, MutablePropertySources ordering (addFirst/addLast). Refresh at runtime: Spring Cloud @RefreshScope + /actuator/refresh or Spring Cloud Bus; plain Boot needs a restart. Values bound with @ConfigurationProperties are rebound on EnvironmentChangeEvent. Secrets: prefer mounted files / Vault; mask them in /actuator/env (management.endpoint.env.show-values=never).

interviewQA: @Value vs @ConfigurationProperties?

@Value injects single values (with SpEL) and is untyped for groups; @ConfigurationProperties binds a prefix to a typed, validated object with nested structures, relaxed binding and metadata, and is preferred for structured settings.
What is the precedence of Boot configuration sources?

Command-line args, system properties, environment variables, profile-specific files, application files, @PropertySource and defaults, in that decreasing order (simplified), so deployment config overrides packaged defaults.
What is relaxed binding?
Boot maps property names written in kebab-case, camelCase, underscore or upper-case env style (MY_APP_PORT) to the same property, easing use of environment variables.

topics.name: Bean Validation (Jakarta Validation), Constraint Annotations and Spring Validator

beginner.content:
Bean Validation basics

• Jakarta Bean Validation (JSR 380; reference implementation Hibernate Validator, in spring-boot-starter-validation) declares constraints on fields/getters/parameters/records: @NotNull, @NotBlank (strings), @NotEmpty (collections/strings), @Size, @Min/@Max, @Positive/@PositiveOrZero, @DecimalMin, @Digits, @Email, @Pattern, @Past/@Future/@PastOrPresent, @AssertTrue, container-element constraints List<@NotBlank String>. Spring wires a LocalValidatorFactoryBean (Validator + MessageSource integration).

intermediate.content:
Custom constraints and cross-field validation

• Create an annotation with @Constraint(validatedBy = ...) and implement ConstraintValidator<A, T> (the validator can be a Spring bean with injection: Spring's SpringConstraintValidatorFactory). Class-level constraints validate relations between fields (endDate > startDate, password confirmation). Groups (@Validated(OnCreate.class)) apply different rules per use case. Avoid database lookups in validators on hot paths (race conditions): enforce uniqueness with a DB constraint too.

expert.content:
Spring's Validator interface

• The older Spring-specific org.springframework.validation.Validator (supports(Class) + validate(Object, Errors)) works with DataBinder, Errors/BindingResult and ValidationUtils.rejectIfEmptyOrWhitespace. Use for validation that is awkward with annotations; register via @InitBinder in MVC. SpringValidatorAdapter bridges Bean Validation to it.

interviewQA: @NotNull vs @NotEmpty vs @NotBlank?
@NotNull rejects null; @NotEmpty rejects null and empty strings/collections; @NotBlank applies to strings and also rejects whitespace-only values.
How do you write a custom validation annotation?
Define an annotation meta-annotated with @Constraint and implement ConstraintValidator; the validator can use Spring injection, and class-level constraints cover cross-field rules.
Bean Validation vs Spring Validator?
Bean Validation is the standard annotation-driven approach (Hibernate Validator); Spring's Validator interface is programmatic and works with Errors/BindingResult; Spring integrates both.

topics.name: @Valid vs @Validated, Method Validation, Groups and Validation Error Handling

beginner.content:
@Valid vs @Validated

@Valid (jakarta.validation)@Validated (Spring)
SourceJakarta standardSpring
Validation groupsNoYes
Cascading to nested objectsYes (on the field)No (use @Valid on the field)
On a class (method validation)NoYes: enables validation of method parameters/returns of that bean via a proxy
Typical use@RequestBody @Valid, nested fieldsGroups, class-level method validation, @ConfigurationProperties

intermediate.content:
Method validation and controller validation

• Put @Validated on a bean class and constraints on method parameters/return values: Spring's MethodValidationPostProcessor (AOP proxy) throws ConstraintViolationException on violation (proxy rules apply: external calls only). Spring 6.1 adds built-in method validation for controllers (HandlerMethodValidationException). For request bodies, @Valid @RequestBody throws MethodArgumentNotValidException; for @RequestParam/@PathVariable constraints use @Validated on the controller (ConstraintViolationException).

expert.content:
Validation error handling

• Convert violations to a consistent API error: @RestControllerAdvice handling MethodArgumentNotValidException (field errors from BindingResult), ConstraintViolationException, HandlerMethodValidationException; return RFC 9457 ProblemDetail with a field → message map and HTTP 400 (or 422).
