Never leak internals; localise messages (MessageSource + {key} in annotations). Validate at the edge (DTOs) and enforce invariants again in the domain/database (constraints). Don't validate entities with request-level groups scattered everywhere: use DTOs per use case.

interviewQA: @Valid vs @Validated?

@Valid is the Jakarta standard that triggers validation and cascades to nested objects; @Validated is Spring's variant that supports validation groups and enables method-level validation when placed on a class.
How do you handle validation errors in a REST API?
Handle MethodArgumentNotValidException and ConstraintViolationException in a @RestControllerAdvice and return a 400 ProblemDetail with field-level messages.
Why is @Validated on a service class sometimes ignored?
Method validation is proxy-based, so internal self-calls, non-public methods, or classes that are not Spring beans are not validated.

topics.name: Transaction Fundamentals, ACID, Transaction Managers and Declarative vs Programmatic

beginner.content:
Transaction fundamentals

• A transaction groups operations into one unit that either completely succeeds or has no effect. ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (valid state to valid state), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not see each other's partial work, with levels), Durability (committed data survives crashes).
• Spring's transaction abstraction offers one consistent programming model across JDBC, JPA/Hibernate, JMS, JTA: PlatformTransactionManager (getTransaction, commit, rollback) implementations: DataSourceTransactionManager (JDBC/JdbcTemplate/MyBatis), JpaTransactionManager (JPA/Hibernate: Boot picks it), JtaTransactionManager (distributed XA), R2dbcTransactionManager/ReactiveTransactionManager. A transaction is bound to the current thread (TransactionSynchronizationManager, holding the connection/EntityManager in thread-locals).

intermediate.content:
Declarative (@Transactional) vs programmatic (TransactionTemplate)

Declarative @TransactionalProgrammatic TransactionTemplate / PlatformTransactionManager
StyleAnnotation + AOP proxyCode (lambda callback)
BoundariesWhole methodPrecise sub-method scope
Self-invocationBypasses the proxyWorks anywhere
Dynamic settingsFixed per methodChoose propagation/isolation at runtime
UseDefault for servicesBatches, self-calls, fine-grained scope, non-proxied code
• Enable with @EnableTransactionManagement (Boot auto-configures it with spring-boot-starter-data-jpa/jdbc). Apply @Transactional on the service layer (use-case boundary), not on controllers or repositories.

expert.content:
How @Transactional works (proxy) and enabling it

• @Transactional methods are intercepted by TransactionInterceptor: get connection/EntityManager → begin → invoke method → on success commit, on exception rollback per rules → release resources. It needs public methods called through the proxy; self-invocation, final/private methods and non-bean objects are not transactional. Put the annotation on the implementation class (or its methods). Class-level applies to all public methods; method-level overrides. @Transactional(readOnly = true) at class level with writes overridden is a common pattern.

interviewQA: What are the ACID properties?

Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (valid state transitions), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere according to the isolation level) and Durability (committed data survives failures).
Declarative vs programmatic transactions?

Declarative uses @Transactional via an AOP proxy and is the default; programmatic uses TransactionTemplate/PlatformTransactionManager for fine-grained scope, runtime-chosen settings and self-invocation cases.
Where should @Transactional be placed?
On service-layer methods or classes representing a use case, on public methods called from outside through the proxy; not on controllers or repositories.

topics.name: Transaction Propagation Levels and Isolation Levels

beginner.content:
Propagation: what happens when a transactional method calls another

PropagationIf a transaction existsIf none exists
REQUIRED (default)Join itCreate new
REQUIRES_NEWSuspend it, run in a new independent oneCreate new
SUPPORTSJoin itRun non-transactionally
NOT_SUPPORTEDSuspend it, run non-transactionallyRun non-transactionally
MANDATORYJoin itThrow IllegalTransactionStateException
NEVERThrowRun non-transactionally
NESTEDRun in a savepoint (inner rollback does not roll back the outer; JDBC only, not JPA by default)Create new
• REQUIRED: inner and outer share one physical transaction: if the inner method throws and marks it rollback-only, the outer cannot commit (UnexpectedRollbackException, "Transaction silently rolled back because it has been marked as rollback-only"). REQUIRES_NEW: independent commit/rollback: use for audit logging that must persist even when the main transaction fails.

intermediate.content:
Isolation levels and concurrency anomalies

LevelDirty readNon-repeatable readPhantom read
READ_UNCOMMITTEDPossiblePossiblePossible
READ_COMMITTED (PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server default)NoPossiblePossible
REPEATABLE_READ (MySQL InnoDB default)NoNoPossible (prevented in InnoDB/PostgreSQL)
SERIALIZABLENoNoNo (slowest; retries on conflict)
DEFAULTUse the database's default level
• Dirty read: reading another transaction's uncommitted data. Non-repeatable read: same row read twice gives different values. Phantom: a repeated query returns new rows. Higher isolation = fewer anomalies, lower concurrency. Isolation applies when a new transaction starts (ignored by an inner REQUIRED that joins). For concurrent updates also use optimistic locking (@Version) or pessimistic locks (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE).

expert.content:
Timeout and read-only

• timeout (seconds) aborts long transactions (applied by the driver/connection). readOnly = true is a hint: Hibernate skips dirty checking (flush mode MANUAL) and some drivers/routers send the query to a read replica; it does not prevent writes in every database. Use it for query-only service methods to save memory and CPU.
codeExamples:
@Transactional(readOnly = true, timeout = 5)
public Page<CourseDto> search(CourseQuery q, Pageable p) { ... }

interviewQA: Explain transaction propagation.

It defines what a transactional method does when called inside or outside an existing transaction: REQUIRED joins or creates (default), REQUIRES_NEW suspends and starts an independent one, NESTED uses a savepoint, MANDATORY/NEVER enforce presence/absence, SUPPORTS and NOT_SUPPORTED are lenient.
REQUIRED vs REQUIRES_NEW?
REQUIRED shares one transaction so a rollback in either rolls back both; REQUIRES_NEW suspends the outer and commits or rolls back independently, e.g. for audit records.
What are isolation levels and the anomalies they prevent?
READ_UNCOMMITTED, READ_COMMITTED, REPEATABLE_READ and SERIALIZABLE progressively prevent dirty reads, non-repeatable reads and phantom reads at the cost of concurrency.

topics.name: Rollback Rules, Common @Transactional Pitfalls, Transaction Synchronization and Distributed Transactions

beginner.content:
Rollback rules

• By default Spring rolls back on unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException) and Error; checked exceptions commit the transaction! Customise: rollbackFor = Exception.class, noRollbackFor = BusinessWarning.class (also rollbackForClassName). Programmatic: TransactionAspectSupport.currentTransactionStatus().setRollbackOnly().
• Catching and swallowing an exception inside the method prevents rollback (the interceptor never sees it). If an inner REQUIRED call throws and you catch it outside, the shared transaction is already rollback-only: the outer commit throws UnexpectedRollbackException.

intermediate.content:
Common @Transactional pitfalls checklist

PitfallFix
Self-invocation / calling from the same classMove to another bean or use TransactionTemplate
Non-public, final or private methodMake public, non-final
Checked exception does not roll backrollbackFor = Exception.class
Exception swallowed in the methodRethrow or setRollbackOnly()
Wrong @Transactional (javax/jakarta.transaction vs Spring)Use org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional for full features
Transaction on a new thread (@Async, parallel streams)Transactions are thread-bound: start a transaction inside the async method
Long transactions (remote calls, user waits inside)Keep transactions short, do I/O outside
Lazy loading outside the transaction (LazyInitializationException)Fetch needed data inside (join fetch, DTO projection), avoid open-session-in-view
Multiple data sources, wrong manager@Transactional("ordersTm")
Calling REQUIRES_NEW expecting an outer read to see its rowsUnderstand isolation (outer cannot see uncommitted/new snapshot)

expert.content:
Transaction synchronization and distributed transactions

• TransactionSynchronizationManager.registerSynchronization(new TransactionSynchronization() { afterCommit() ... }) runs code at transaction phases (what @TransactionalEventListener uses): send messages only after a successful commit. Distributed transactions: XA/JTA (Atomikos, Narayana; 2PC: slow, rarely used in microservices). Preferred: local transactions + the Saga pattern (orchestrated or choreographed) with transactional outbox (write the event in the same local transaction, publish asynchronously) and idempotent consumers. ChainedTransactionManager was removed (best-effort, unsafe).

interviewQA: Does a checked exception roll back a Spring transaction?
Not by default: only RuntimeException and Error trigger rollback; use rollbackFor = Exception.class to include checked exceptions.
Why does @Transactional on a private method not work?
Transactions are applied by proxies that intercept public method calls from outside; private methods are never intercepted, so no transaction starts.
How do you handle transactions across microservices?
Avoid 2PC; use local transactions with the Saga pattern, a transactional outbox and idempotent consumers for eventual consistency.

subTopics.name: Phase 16 · Spring JDBC and Data Access (Core)

topics.name: JdbcTemplate, NamedParameterJdbcTemplate, JdbcClient, RowMapper and Batch Operations

beginner.content:
Why Spring JDBC?

• Raw JDBC needs boilerplate: open connection, prepare statement, bind, execute, map rows, close everything, translate SQLException. JdbcTemplate removes it: it acquires/releases connections, executes, maps rows and translates exceptions into Spring's unchecked DataAccessException hierarchy. You supply only the SQL and the mapping. Starter: spring-boot-starter-jdbc (HikariCP DataSource auto-configured from spring.datasource.*).

intermediate.content:
NamedParameterJdbcTemplate, SimpleJdbcInsert and JdbcClient

• NamedParameterJdbcTemplate uses :name placeholders (readable; MapSqlParameterSource, BeanPropertySqlParameterSource, IN lists expand automatically). SimpleJdbcInsert builds inserts from table metadata (and returns generated keys); SimpleJdbcCall calls stored procedures. JdbcClient (Spring 6.1) is a fluent facade over both: sql(...).param(...).query(Type).list()/optional()/single().
• Always use bound parameters, never string concatenation: that prevents SQL injection.

expert.content:
RowMapper, ResultSetExtractor and batch operations

• RowMapper<T> maps one row to an object (reusable); ResultSetExtractor processes the whole result (grouping parent/child rows); RowCallbackHandler streams rows with no result list (large data); BeanPropertyRowMapper/DataClassRowMapper map by column names. Batch: batchUpdate(sql, BatchPreparedStatementSetter | List<Object[]> | SqlParameterSource[]) sends many statements in one round-trip: set reWriteBatchedInserts=true (PostgreSQL) for speed; chunk big batches.

interviewQA: What does JdbcTemplate give you over plain JDBC?
It manages connections and resources, executes SQL, offers row mapping and batch helpers and translates SQLException into the DataAccessException hierarchy, so you write only the SQL and mapping.
Why prefer named parameters?
They make SQL readable, support IN-list expansion and bean binding and still use prepared statements, protecting against SQL injection.
When use ResultSetExtractor instead of RowMapper?
When you must process the entire result set at once, e.g. to assemble parent/child object graphs from a join.

topics.name: DataSource, Connection Pooling, Transactions with JDBC and Exception Translation

beginner.content:
DataSource and connection pooling

• A DataSource hands out connections. Never use DriverManagerDataSource in production (new connection per call). Use a connection pool: HikariCP (Boot default): maximumPoolSize (default 10), minimumIdle, connectionTimeout (30s), idleTimeout, maxLifetime (shorter than DB/ proxy timeout), leakDetectionThreshold. Pool sizing: small pools perform best (connections ≈ cores × 2 + disks); size to what the database can serve across all application instances.
codeExamples:
# application.yml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/jsl
    username: ${DB_USER}
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD}
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 20
      minimum-idle: 5
      connection-timeout: 3000
      max-lifetime: 1500000          # 25 min < DB/proxy idle timeout
      leak-detection-threshold: 20000
      pool-name: jsl-pool

@Bean DataSource dataSource(DataSourceProperties props) { return props.initializeDataSourceBuilder().type(HikariDataSource.class).build(); }

intermediate.content:
JDBC transactions and transaction-aware connections

• DataSourceTransactionManager binds one Connection to the thread for the duration of the transaction; JdbcTemplate obtains it through DataSourceUtils.getConnection, so every DAO call inside the same @Transactional method uses the same connection and transaction. If you use dataSource.getConnection() directly you bypass this: always wrap with DataSourceUtils or use the template. Use TransactionAwareDataSourceProxy for legacy code. Multiple data sources need separate transaction managers and qualifiers.

expert.content:
Exception translation: the DataAccessException hierarchy

• Spring converts vendor-specific SQLException/JPA/Hibernate exceptions into a technology-neutral, unchecked hierarchy rooted at DataAccessException: DuplicateKeyException / DataIntegrityViolationException (constraint), EmptyResultDataAccessException (queryForObject found none), IncorrectResultSizeDataAccessException, DataAccessResourceFailureException, CannotAcquireLockException, DeadlockLoserDataAccessException, OptimisticLockingFailureException, QueryTimeoutException, BadSqlGrammarException. Translators: SQLErrorCodeSQLExceptionTranslator (uses vendor error codes), SQLStateSQLExceptionTranslator; JPA repositories get translation from @Repository + PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor. Separate transient (retry) from non-transient failures.

interviewQA: What is exception translation?

Converting vendor-specific persistence exceptions into Spring's unchecked DataAccessException hierarchy so the service layer is independent of JDBC/JPA/Hibernate details; @Repository beans get it automatically.
How do you size a HikariCP pool?
Keep it small, based on what the database can process concurrently (roughly cores×2 + disks), multiplied by application instances, and tune timeouts and max lifetime below infrastructure idle limits.
Why must JDBC code use the template or DataSourceUtils inside a transaction?
They enlist in the thread-bound transaction connection; opening a connection directly from the DataSource bypasses the transaction and acts autonomously.

topics.name: ORM Integration, Repository/DAO Patterns and Data Access Best Practices

beginner.content:
ORM integration and repositories

• Spring integrates JPA/Hibernate (LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBean, JpaTransactionManager, shared EntityManager proxy via @PersistenceContext), MyBatis, jOOQ. Spring Data generates repository implementations from interfaces (JpaRepository, derived queries, @Query, projections, paging, specifications). Choose JdbcTemplate/JdbcClient/jOOQ for set-based SQL, reporting and bulk operations; JPA for rich domain models with CRUD.

intermediate.content:
DAO vs Repository, and data access design

DAORepository
AbstractionWraps a table/data source (technical)Collection of aggregates (domain, DDD)
InterfaceCRUD per tableMethods in domain language (findActiveCourses)
Typical in Spring@Repository with JdbcTemplateSpring Data repositories
• Keep the persistence API behind an interface owned by the domain; do not let entities/JPA types leak into controllers (use DTOs); keep transactions in services; avoid N+1 queries (fetch joins, @EntityGraph, batch size); paginate; use indexes; version schema with Flyway/Liquibase, never ddl-auto=update in production.

expert.content:
Performance and safety checklist for data access

• Fetch only what you need (projections, pagination, select columns), prevent N+1 (join fetch, @EntityGraph, default_batch_fetch_size), use batching for bulk writes, add indexes for query predicates and check plans (EXPLAIN), set timeouts, keep transactions short, use optimistic locking for concurrent updates, version the schema with Flyway/Liquibase, and never concatenate SQL.
codeExamples:
# Hibernate/JPA settings worth knowing
spring.jpa.open-in-view=false                       # avoid lazy loading during view rendering
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.order_inserts=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size=32
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate              # schema is owned by Flyway

interviewQA: JdbcTemplate vs JPA: when to use which?
JdbcTemplate/JdbcClient give full SQL control for reports, bulk and set-based work; JPA/Hibernate suit rich object models with CRUD and relationships; many applications use both in one transaction.
DAO vs Repository?
A DAO is a technical per-table data gateway; a Repository represents a domain collection of aggregates with domain-oriented methods; Spring Data repositories follow the latter style.
What is the N+1 problem?
One query loads N parents and then N additional queries load each child lazily; fix with join fetch, entity graphs, batch fetching or projections.

topics.name: Spring Security Overview: Authentication, Authorization and the Filter Chain

beginner.content:
What Spring Security provides

• Spring Security is a separate project that secures applications: authentication (who are you?), authorization (what may you do?), protection against common attacks (CSRF, session fixation, clickjacking, security headers), password encoding, OAuth2/OIDC/JWT resource server and login, method security. It is built on servlet filters plus AOP method interceptors.
• Core objects: SecurityContext / SecurityContextHolder (thread-bound), Authentication (principal, credentials, authorities, authenticated flag), GrantedAuthority (ROLE_ADMIN, SCOPE_read), UserDetails / UserDetailsService, AuthenticationManager / ProviderManager / AuthenticationProvider, PasswordEncoder.

intermediate.content:
The filter chain

• A request passes through the DelegatingFilterProxy → FilterChainProxy → one SecurityFilterChain (the first whose matcher matches) containing ordered filters: SecurityContextHolderFilter, HeaderWriterFilter, CsrfFilter, LogoutFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter / BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter / BasicAuthenticationFilter, RequestCacheAwareFilter, AnonymousAuthenticationFilter, ExceptionTranslationFilter (401/403 handling), AuthorizationFilter (access decision). Flow: authentication filter → AuthenticationManager → AuthenticationProvider → UserDetailsService + PasswordEncoder → Authentication stored in the SecurityContext; later authorization decides access. Enable debug: logging.level.org.springframework.security=DEBUG.

expert.content:
Multiple filter chains and custom filters

• Define several SecurityFilterChain beans ordered with @Order and a securityMatcher (e.g. a stateless /api/** chain with JWT and a session-based chain for the admin UI). Add custom filters with addFilterBefore/After relative to a known filter (for API keys, tenant resolution, request ids). Remember that filter order matters and that Spring Security 6 requires explicit authorizeHttpRequests rules (deny by default is recommended).

interviewQA: Authentication vs authorization?
Authentication verifies identity (login, token); authorization decides what an authenticated principal may access (roles, authorities, rules).
How does Spring Security work internally?

A chain of servlet filters authenticates the request through an AuthenticationManager and its providers, stores the Authentication in the SecurityContext (thread-bound) and an authorization filter/method interceptor then makes access decisions.
Role vs authority?
Authority is any granted permission string; a role is an authority with the ROLE_ prefix (hasRole("ADMIN") checks ROLE_ADMIN).

topics.name: UserDetailsService, Password Encoding, Method Security, CSRF and CORS

beginner.content:
UserDetailsService and PasswordEncoder

• UserDetailsService.loadUserByUsername loads the user (database, LDAP); the DaoAuthenticationProvider compares the submitted password with PasswordEncoder.matches. Never store plain text or fast hashes (MD5/SHA-1): use BCryptPasswordEncoder, Argon2, SCrypt or DelegatingPasswordEncoder (PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder(): stores {bcrypt}... to allow algorithm upgrades). Never log passwords or tokens. Pick a work factor that takes ~100–300 ms.

intermediate.content:
Method-level security

• @EnableMethodSecurity activates @PreAuthorize/@PostAuthorize/@PreFilter/@PostFilter (and @Secured, JSR-250 @RolesAllowed), implemented as AOP interceptors, so proxy rules (public, external calls) apply. Use SpEL: hasRole, hasAuthority, #param, authentication.principal, @bean.check(#id), returnObject. Secure at the service layer too (defence in depth), not only URLs.

expert.content:
CSRF, CORS, sessions and common attacks

• CSRF: browsers auto-send cookies, so a malicious site can trigger state-changing requests; Spring Security requires a CSRF token on unsafe methods for session/cookie apps; stateless token (Bearer) APIs can disable it. CORS: configure allowed origins/methods/headers explicitly (CorsConfigurationSource; no * with credentials). Session fixation protection and secure cookies (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite). Security headers on by default (X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, HSTS). Also: OWASP top 10 (injection → parameterised queries, broken access control → deny by default, XSS → output encoding), validate input, rate limit, keep dependencies updated.

interviewQA: How should passwords be stored?
Hashed with a slow, salted algorithm such as bcrypt/Argon2 via a PasswordEncoder (DelegatingPasswordEncoder to allow upgrades), never in plain text or with fast hashes.
What is CSRF and when can you disable it?

An attack that makes a victim's browser send authenticated state-changing requests; protection uses tokens. For stateless APIs authenticated with Bearer tokens (not cookies) CSRF protection can be disabled.
@PreAuthorize vs URL security?
URL rules protect endpoints at the web layer; @PreAuthorize protects service methods via AOP and supports SpEL, giving defence in depth.

topics.name: Testing Strategy: Unit Tests with Constructor Injection and Mockito

beginner.content:
Test pyramid for Spring applications

• Most tests should be fast plain unit tests (no Spring context): this is the main payoff of constructor injection: new Service(fakeRepo). Then slice tests (@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest, @JsonTest) loading only part of the context, then a few full integration tests (@SpringBootTest with Testcontainers). Use JUnit 5 + Mockito + AssertJ (included by spring-boot-starter-test).

intermediate.content:
Testing guidelines

• Test behaviour, not implementation; one assertion concept per test; deterministic (inject Clock, random seeds); no shared mutable state; do not mock what you own heavily (prefer fakes/in-memory implementations); never mock the class under test. Parameterise with @ParameterizedTest.

expert.content:
Testing without Spring but with real wiring

• You can also assemble a small object graph by hand (constructor injection) for component tests, or create a tiny AnnotationConfigApplicationContext with only the classes under test. This keeps tests in milliseconds while still exercising real collaboration between two or three classes. Use test data builders and fakes (in-memory repositories) rather than long Mockito stubbing chains.

interviewQA: Why does constructor injection improve testability?
The class can be instantiated with test doubles using new, with no container, reflection or setters, making unit tests fast and simple.
What is the test pyramid?
Many fast unit tests, fewer slice/integration tests and a small number of end-to-end tests, balancing speed and confidence.

topics.name: Spring TestContext Framework, @SpringBootTest, Slice Tests and @MockBean

beginner.content:
TestContext framework

• spring-test integrates the container with JUnit 5: @ExtendWith(SpringExtension.class) (included in Boot's annotations), @ContextConfiguration, @ActiveProfiles, @TestPropertySource, @DirtiesContext, @Sql, @Transactional on tests (auto-rollback), @DynamicPropertySource. The context is cached across tests with the same configuration: avoid unnecessary variations (different @MockBean sets, properties) to keep the suite fast.

intermediate.content:
Slice tests and mocking beans

AnnotationLoadsUse for
@WebMvcTest(Controller.class)MVC layer, MockMvc, security filters, JSON; no servicesControllers, validation, error handling
@DataJpaTestJPA repositories, embedded/Testcontainers DB, rollbackQueries, mappings
@JdbcTestJdbcTemplate + DataSourceJDBC DAOs
@JsonTestJacksonSerialisation
@RestClientTestRestClient + MockRestServiceServerHTTP clients
@SpringBootTestWhole applicationWiring and end-to-end flows
• @MockBean / @SpyBean (Boot 3.4+: @MockitoBean / @MockitoSpyBean) replace a bean in the context with a Mockito mock; @TestConfiguration adds test beans; @Import for extra config.

expert.content:
Testing transactions, events, async and time

• @Transactional on a test method rolls back after each test (but hides commit-time behaviour: AFTER_COMMIT listeners don't fire, lazy issues disappear): for those scenarios use non-transactional tests with cleanup. @RecordApplicationEvents verifies events; Awaitility for async; inject a fixed Clock; @Sql("/seed.sql") for data; Testcontainers for real databases instead of H2 differences; @DynamicPropertySource to inject container ports. Keep test configuration small to reuse the cached context.

interviewQA: @WebMvcTest vs @SpringBootTest?
@WebMvcTest loads only the web layer (controllers, MockMvc) for fast focused tests with services mocked; @SpringBootTest loads the full application context for integration tests.
What does @MockBean do?
Adds a Mockito mock to the application context replacing any existing bean of that type, so tests can stub collaborators of the unit under test.
Why is the Spring test context cached and why does it matter?
Contexts with identical configuration are reused across test classes, so avoiding needless variations (different @MockBean sets, properties) keeps the suite fast.

topics.name: Auto-Configuration Internals and Building a Custom Starter

beginner.content:
How auto-configuration works

• @EnableAutoConfiguration imports AutoConfigurationImportSelector, which reads candidate classes from META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports in every jar. Each auto-configuration is a @AutoConfiguration class (a @Configuration) guarded by @ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean (user beans win), @ConditionalOnProperty, ordered by @AutoConfiguration(after=...), exposing @ConfigurationProperties. Debug with --debug or Actuator conditions; exclude with spring.autoconfigure.exclude.

intermediate.content:
Custom starter conventions

• Split into my-lib (the code), my-lib-autoconfigure (auto-configuration + properties metadata via spring-boot-configuration-processor) and my-lib-spring-boot-starter (empty module with dependencies). Name third-party starters acme-spring-boot-starter (the spring-boot-starter-* prefix is reserved). Make everything back off (@ConditionalOnMissingBean), opt-out-able by property, documented, tested with ApplicationContextRunner.

expert.content:
Ordering, exclusions and keeping starters maintainable

• Use @AutoConfiguration(before = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class)/after to control ordering (@ConditionalOnBean only works for beans registered earlier). Provide sensible defaults, support @ConditionalOnProperty(matchIfMissing=true) toggles, publish configuration metadata, keep the starter free of heavy transitive dependencies and version it with the Boot BOM. Provide EnvironmentPostProcessors only when really needed.

interviewQA: How does Spring Boot auto-configuration work?

The AutoConfiguration.imports files list @AutoConfiguration classes that are imported and applied conditionally (on classes, missing beans, properties), so Boot configures sensible defaults that back off when you define your own beans.
How do you write a custom starter?

Provide an autoconfigure module with @AutoConfiguration classes, conditions, @ConfigurationProperties and an imports file, plus a starter module that pulls dependencies; test with ApplicationContextRunner.

topics.name: AOT Processing, GraalVM Native Images, CDS/Virtual Threads and Startup Performance

beginner.content:
AOT processing and native images

• Spring 6 / Boot 3 AOT (spring-boot:process-aot) analyses the application at build time: generates bean-definition code (no classpath scanning or CGLIB at runtime), and runtime hints for reflection/proxies/resources. With GraalVM (mvn -Pnative native:compile, or bootBuildImage with buildpacks) you get a native executable: milliseconds startup, lower memory, but longer builds, closed-world constraints (no dynamic classpath changes, profiles/conditions fixed at build time) and fewer libraries supported. JVM alternatives: CRaC (checkpoint/restore), CDS/AppCDS (-XX:SharedArchiveFile, Boot 3.3 support), virtual threads (spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true) for throughput on blocking I/O.
codeExamples:
# native image via buildpacks
mvn -Pnative spring-boot:build-image
# or
mvn -Pnative native:compile && ./target/catalogue

# JVM startup tuning
java -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 -Xshare:auto -jar app.jar
spring.main.lazy-initialization=true         # faster startup, slower first request
spring.jmx.enabled=false

intermediate.content:
Finding and reducing startup cost

• Measure first: /actuator/startup with BufferingApplicationStartup, -Ddebug timings, spring.main.log-startup-info. Reduce: narrow @ComponentScan, remove unused starters/auto-configurations (spring.autoconfigure.exclude), avoid heavy work in @PostConstruct, lazy beans for rarely used features, avoid classpath scanning of huge packages, exclude unused JPA entity scanning. Keep the singleton-bean graph small and moves slow initialisation out of startup (ApplicationReadyEvent in the background).

expert.content:
Native image and AOT: practical rules

• Keep reflection explicit: register hints with @RegisterReflectionForBinding for DTOs serialised by Jackson, and use RuntimeHintsPredicates to test hints. Avoid runtime classpath scanning, dynamic proxies of unknown interfaces and Class.forName on strings. Run the application tests in native mode in CI (nativeTest) because behaviour can differ. Decide per service: native for scale-to-zero/serverless, JVM plus CDS/virtual threads for long-lived services.

interviewQA: What does Spring AOT do?

It processes the application at build time, generating optimised bean definition code and runtime hints (reflection, proxies, resources) so the app starts faster and can be compiled into a GraalVM native image.
What are the trade-offs of GraalVM native images?
Very fast startup and low memory in exchange for longer builds, closed-world restrictions (build-time decisions on conditions/profiles, reflection hints) and limited library support.

topics.name: Design Patterns in Spring, Programmatic Registration, Modularity and Spring Modulith

beginner.content:
Design patterns used by Spring

PatternWhere in Spring
Singleton / Prototype / FactoryBean scopes, BeanFactory, FactoryBean
ProxyAOP, @Transactional, scoped and lazy proxies
Template methodJdbcTemplate, TransactionTemplate, RestTemplate, AbstractApplicationContext.refresh
ObserverApplication events
StrategyResourceLoader, PlatformTransactionManager, HandlerMapping, PasswordEncoder
Decorator / Chain of responsibilityBeanPostProcessor, servlet filter chain, interceptor chain
AdapterHandlerAdapter, MessageConverter
BuilderBeanDefinitionBuilder, UriComponentsBuilder, HttpSecurity
Dependency Injection / IoCThe container itself
Front controllerDispatcherServlet

intermediate.content:
Programmatic registration (functional bean definitions)

• Spring 5+ offers a functional API (BeanRegistrar in 7, GenericApplicationContext.registerBean with suppliers and BeanDefinitionCustomizer) to register beans without reflection, useful for libraries, tests and native images. ApplicationContextInitializer runs before refresh to register beans/profiles. Use programmatic registration for dynamic, data-driven bean sets (one client per tenant/config entry).

expert.content:
Modularity: Spring Modulith, ArchUnit and clean architecture

• Spring Modulith structures a monolith into application modules (packages), verifies module boundaries (ApplicationModules.of(App.class).verify()), documents them, tests modules in isolation (@ApplicationModuleTest) and provides event externalisation with a persistent event publication registry (a built-in outbox). Pair with ArchUnit rules and hexagonal/clean architecture (domain independent of Spring), and keep module-to-module communication via events or published APIs. A well-modularised monolith can later be split into services.

interviewQA: Which design patterns does Spring use?

Singleton/factory (container), proxy (AOP), template method (JdbcTemplate), observer (events), strategy, decorator/chain (post-processors and filters), adapter and front controller (DispatcherServlet).
What is Spring Modulith?
A toolkit for building modular monoliths: it verifies module boundaries, supports isolated module tests and provides an event publication registry for reliable in-process events.

topics.name: Interview Questions: IoC, DI, Beans, Scopes and Configuration

beginner.content:
How to answer

• State the definition, explain the mechanism (what the container actually does), give a short code example, then mention a pitfall or trade-off. Interviewers care about understanding the why (loose coupling, proxies, lifecycle), not memorised annotation lists.

intermediate.content:
Rapid-fire recap: IoC and beans

QuestionOne-line answer
IoC vs DIIoC is the principle (framework controls creation/wiring); DI is the technique that supplies dependencies
Best injection styleConstructor: immutable, mandatory, testable
Default scopeSingleton (one per container)
Default proxy type in BootCGLIB
@Component vs @BeanClass-level scanning vs method-level factory (third-party/custom creation)
@Primary vs @QualifierDefault candidate vs explicit choice at the injection point (qualifier wins)
Circular dependencyConstructor cycles fail; redesign or @Lazy; Boot forbids field cycles by default

expert.content:
Coding questions asked live

• Write a service with constructor injection and a unit test with a mock. • Show two implementations of one interface and select one with @Qualifier, @Primary and a profile. • Create a custom scope or a prototype injected correctly into a singleton. • Fix a circular dependency. • Explain what happens when two beans share a name. Practise explaining aloud what the container does at each step.

interviewQA: What is Spring and why use it?

A framework whose IoC container wires POJOs together and which provides AOP, transactions, data access, web and testing support; benefits are loose coupling, testability, declarative infrastructure and consistent abstractions.
Explain IoC and dependency injection with an example.

Instead of a class creating its dependencies, the container creates and injects them (e.g. a service receiving a repository in its constructor), so implementations can be swapped and tested with fakes.
BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext?
BeanFactory is the minimal lazy container; ApplicationContext adds eager singletons, post-processor auto-registration, events, i18n, resources and Environment, and is what applications use.
What are the bean scopes?
singleton, prototype, request, session, application, websocket and custom scopes.
Constructor vs setter vs field injection?
Constructor for mandatory immutable dependencies (preferred), setter for optional, field injection discouraged because it hides dependencies and hampers testing.
How does Spring resolve ambiguity between beans of the same type?
By @Qualifier at the injection point, then @Primary, then @Priority and finally by matching the injection point name to a bean name.
What is a singleton bean in Spring and is it thread-safe?
One shared instance per container; Spring does not make it thread-safe, so keep it stateless or synchronise shared state.
How do you inject a prototype into a singleton?
Use ObjectProvider/Provider, @Lookup or a scoped proxy so a new instance is obtained at each use.
@Configuration vs @Component?
@Configuration classes are CGLIB-enhanced so @Bean method calls return container-managed singletons; in a @Component (lite mode) they behave as plain method calls.
How does component scanning work?
ClassPathBeanDefinitionScanner finds classes with stereotype annotations in the given packages and registers them as bean definitions.

topics.name: Interview Questions: Lifecycle, Post-Processors, AOP and Proxies

beginner.content:
Key diagrams to draw in interviews

• Bean lifecycle: instantiate → inject → Aware → BPP before → @PostConstruct → afterPropertiesSet → init-method → BPP after (proxy) → use → @PreDestroy → destroy → destroy-method.
• Proxy call path: caller → proxy → interceptor chain (security → transaction → cache → custom) → target. Self-invocation skips the proxy.

intermediate.content:
Common traps

• "Why doesn't @Transactional work?" (self-invocation, private/final, checked exception, wrong thread, swallowed exception, proxy not created). • "Does prototype get @PreDestroy?" (no). • "Is @Order the creation order?" (no). • "Can parent contexts see child beans?" (no). • "JDK proxy injected by class?" (fails). • "What does readOnly=true guarantee?" (a hint, not a write ban).

expert.content:
Advanced follow-ups interviewers ask

• "Where exactly is the proxy created and which bean does the container hold?" (postProcessAfterInitialization of the auto-proxy creator; the container holds the proxy.) • "How would you implement your own @Retry?" (an aspect with @Around and ordering outside the transaction.) • "Why are BPP beans created early?" (they must exist before regular beans.) • "How does @Configuration inter-bean call interception work?" (CGLIB subclass overriding @Bean methods to consult the container.)

interviewQA: Explain the Spring bean lifecycle.

Definition loaded and BFPPs run; bean instantiated; dependencies injected; Aware callbacks; BPP before-init; @PostConstruct, afterPropertiesSet, custom init; BPP after-init (AOP proxy); ready; on shutdown @PreDestroy, destroy(), custom destroy.
BeanPostProcessor vs BeanFactoryPostProcessor?
BFPP changes bean definitions before instantiation; BPP intercepts bean instances around initialisation and can return wrappers such as proxies.
What is AOP and where does Spring use it?
Modularising cross-cutting concerns through proxies; used by @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async, security and validation.
JDK proxy vs CGLIB?
JDK proxies implement interfaces; CGLIB subclasses the class (not final); Boot defaults to CGLIB.
What are advice types and pointcut designators?
@Before, @AfterReturning, @AfterThrowing, @After, @Around; execution, within, this/target, args, @annotation, @within, bean.
Why does self-invocation bypass AOP?
this refers to the target not the proxy, so the interceptor chain is skipped.
How do Spring events work?
ApplicationEventPublisher publishes events synchronously to @EventListener/ApplicationListener beans; @Async and @TransactionalEventListener alter threading and timing.
What is SpEL?
An expression language to query/manipulate object graphs at runtime used in @Value, conditions, caching and security.
How does Spring Boot auto-configuration work?
Conditional @AutoConfiguration classes listed in imports files create default beans that back off when you define your own.
What happens at startup in refresh()?
Load definitions, run BFPPs (including @Configuration parsing), register BPPs, init events/i18n, instantiate singletons, start lifecycle beans and publish ContextRefreshedEvent.

topics.name: Interview Questions: Transactions, Data Access, Security, Testing and Scenarios

beginner.content:
Scenario-style answers

• "Payment succeeded but the order was rolled back" → payment call inside the DB transaction: use outbox/saga, idempotency keys and compensation; do external calls after commit.
• "Audit row must persist even when the main operation fails" → REQUIRES_NEW in a separate bean.
• "Slow startup" → measure with startup endpoint, narrow scanning, lazy init, AOT/CDS.
• "Intermittent LazyInitializationException" → access lazy data inside the transaction or use projections; avoid open-session-in-view.

Debugging a transaction problem step by step

• 1) Is the bean a proxy (AopUtils.isAopProxy)? 2) Is the call external (not self-invocation)? 3) Is the method public and non-final? 4) Which exception type and does it match rollback rules? 5) Is the correct transaction manager used? 6) Enable logging.level.org.springframework.transaction.interceptor=TRACE and org.springframework.orm.jpa=DEBUG to see begin/commit/rollback. 7) Check connection pool exhaustion if requests hang inside transactions.

interviewQA: How does @Transactional work internally?

A proxy with TransactionInterceptor obtains a transaction from the PlatformTransactionManager, invokes the method, commits or rolls back according to the exception rules and releases resources; state is thread-bound.
Propagation REQUIRED vs REQUIRES_NEW vs NESTED?
REQUIRED joins or creates; REQUIRES_NEW suspends and creates independent; NESTED uses a savepoint inside the outer transaction.
What are the isolation levels?
READ_UNCOMMITTED, READ_COMMITTED, REPEATABLE_READ, SERIALIZABLE, trading anomalies prevented against concurrency.
Why does a checked exception not roll back?
Spring follows EJB convention: only unchecked exceptions roll back by default; configure rollbackFor to change it.
What is UnexpectedRollbackException?
Thrown when a participating transaction marked the shared transaction rollback-only and the outer scope tried to commit, often after an exception was caught and ignored.
How do you handle distributed transactions?
Avoid XA; use sagas, outbox and idempotent consumers for eventual consistency.
What is exception translation?
Converting persistence exceptions into the DataAccessException hierarchy so higher layers are independent of the data technology.
How do you test a Spring Boot application?
Unit tests with Mockito and constructor injection, slice tests (@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest), and a few @SpringBootTest integration tests with Testcontainers.
How do you secure a REST API in Spring?
A SecurityFilterChain with stateless JWT/OAuth2 resource server, authorisation rules and method security, CSRF disabled for token-only APIs, CORS configured explicitly and bcrypt for passwords.
How do you make a Spring Boot application start faster?
Narrow scanning, remove unused auto-configurations, lazy initialisation for heavy beans, avoid slow @PostConstruct, use AOT/native images or CDS, and measure with the startup endpoint.

cheatNotes: Framework - Provides the common plumbing every application needs, so you write only the business part
Spring - Created by Rod Johnson, released 2003
Tight coupling - A class creates its collaborator with new, so swapping it means editing that class
Loose coupling - A class holds an interface reference and the collaborator is handed in from outside
IoC - Inversion of Control: the container, not your code, creates and assembles objects
DI - Dependency Injection: the technique Spring uses to implement IoC
IoC container duties - Read config, instantiate beans, manage the lifecycle, inject values
POJO - Plain Old Java Object; a Spring bean extends nothing and implements nothing
BeanFactory - Core container, lazy; creates a bean when getBean() is called
XmlBeanFactory - BeanFactory implementation (deprecated 3.1, removed in Spring 5)
ApplicationContext - J2EE container, eager; creates singletons at startup
ClassPathXmlApplicationContext - ApplicationContext implementation taking the XML file name
ClassPathResource - Wraps a classpath file as a Resource for XmlBeanFactory
Eager vs lazy - Eager fails fast at startup; lazy defers the failure to the first request
Bean scopes - singleton (default), prototype, request, session, application
singleton - One instance per container, not the GoF Singleton pattern
prototype - New instance per request; never created at startup in either container
Bean lifecycle - constructor, injection, @PostConstruct, in use, @PreDestroy
@PostConstruct - Runs after dependencies are injected; the constructor is too early
src/main/resources - The only correct home for spring.xml (Maven puts it on the classpath)
pom.xml - Maven Project Object Model: dependencies, plugins, build config
groupId - Project group id, unique across the organisation
artifactId - The project name
spring-core - The IoC container itself
spring-context - ApplicationContext, events, i18n, annotation config
Dependency Injection - Passing required input from the config file into the bean class
Setter injection - <property name="x" value="y"/>; needs a setter
Constructor injection - <constructor-arg value="y"/>; needs a parameterised constructor
constructor-arg index - Pins a value to a parameter position; needed when types are ambiguous
constructor-arg name - Clearest form, but needs javac -parameters
value vs ref - value injects a literal; ref injects another bean by id
Constructor injection preferred - Fields can be final, object is never half-built
Circular dependency - Fails fast with constructor injection; patched up with setter injection
Autowiring - The container injects object dependencies without a ref= line
autowire="byType" - Matches property type against bean class; ignores the bean id
autowire="byName" - Matches property name against bean id; ignores the type
autowire="constructor" - Matches constructor parameters by type
autowire="autodetect" - Removed in Spring 4.0; constructor first, else byType
Autowiring limitation - Cannot inject primitives, only reference types
XML autowiring fails silently - No match means the field stays null until an NPE
@Autowired - Injects by type; the field name only breaks a tie
@Qualifier - Names the bean to use when several match by type
@Primary - Marks one candidate as the default for its type
@Resource - JSR-250; matches by name first, then by type
ObjectProvider - Lazy lookup; the fix for a prototype injected into a singleton
